A.1.c Resettlement: All resettlements on NR1B and NR6A were fully paid by GoL in accordance with Law and Regulations prior to the start of constructions. Page 10 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report A.1.d Supervision consultants: SweRoad in association with WSP and Burapha were assigned as supervision consultant for road upgrading on National Roads 1B and 6A, The Consultant has also assisted DoR in reviewing the detailed bridge designs and Drawings, including bidding documents, for the 6 small bridges and Nam Ma bridge in NR6A which were prepared by LTEC. LTEC, under a separate contract with MPWT, has carried out the topographic surveys, geotechnical investigations, detailed design of the 7 bridges in NR6A. Draft bidding documents, including Drawings and BOQ have been submitted by LTEC to DOR and copied to World Bank. The Team Leader and his team have reviewed LTEC’s design of the bridge structures including their foundations and confirmed/modified to comply with the technical standards and AASHTO LRFD bridge design specifications. He also assisted LTEC in preparing the bidding documents and specifications for the steel structures. Please refer to Appendix E for the final quarterly report of consultant as at December 2015.

A.1.e Monitoring and evaluation: Monitoring and evaluation was performed by Project managers who were assigned by DoR to carry out day-to-day monitoring together with supervision consultants. 4.1.2 Provincial Network Maintenance A.2.a Periodic maintenance and spot improvements: As at 30 September 2017, more than 2,400 km of provincial road have received spot improvement and periodic maintenance under the Project (see Appendix D for provincial road maintenance contracts). Furthermore, in order to cope with the maintenance needs while preventing the road network from further deteriorated and not to lose the momentum while those needs have already been prioritized systematically for the 3-Year Rolling Plan, DoR therefore has received approval by minister for continuing to allocate fund from RMF amount to LAK 41,674.90 million, covering 18 maintenance contracts for provincial roads, with total length of about 300.93 km, spreading allover 18 provinces countrywide. A.2.b Supervision: Supervision was performed by MPWT and DPWT staffs who were assigned by DoR to carry out day-to-day supervision together with provincial and rural management consultants. A.2.c Capacity building: To further strengthen DPWT in managing provincial roads maintenance, a training has been provided to six provinces on planning, supervision, and contract management.

DOR conducted the technical trainings using the remaining training budget and IOC for 12 provinces (Northern and Southern parts) in September 2017. 4.1.3 Road Safety A.3.a Road safety – goods: Package 1 for mitigation of traffic accidents in Vientiane Capital of USD0.58 million and Package 2 for road furniture, road marking and signage on NR13N amounting to USD0.81 million was fully installed. The final 10% payment for Package 2 was made in February 2016. A.3.b Road safety – awareness and capacity building: The public campaign in Vientiane Capital and traffic management training have been successfully completed while the speed management training had been postponed from November 2015 to January 2016 due to the readiness of AIT. However, the speed management training had been again postponed and conducted on 14-17 June 2016 while the awareness raising was shifted from NR13N to NR1B and NR6A which expects to be Page 11 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report carried out in October-November 2016. Due to the minimal readiness of the communities, the actual implementation is reset to perform in February 2017. Procurement for the safety capacity assessment consultant, who will help on updating traffic regulation and fine decree and PRSC workshops are postponed due to the budget constraints (see Appendix E for details).

4.2 Institutional Strengthening 4.2.1 Strategic management B.1.a Strategic management advisory and capacity development: Strategic Planning and Management (SPM) Consultant Services: Strategic Planning and Management Final Report has been utilized as the basis to produce the Sector 8th Five-Year Plan (2016-2020), Strategy up to 2025 and Vision up to 2030. The Five-Year Plan (FYP) in Lao version has been finalized and received the minister’s approval. The available edition of the FYP can be shared to all development partners. Public-Private Partnership (PPP) financing of roads: ToRs for individual consultants and a firm on ESIA, RAP and EGDP have been completed. Two individual consultants have been on board since July 2016, however, due to budget constraint resulting delays in procuring a consulting firm to perform additional surveys. Therefore, all E&S related studies were carried out under Lao Road Sector Project 2. MPWT reported the progress of PPP to the government on 11 August 2016, and it has been agreed that a full report, including response to government enquiries on 7 issues, from MPWT to the government on the way to have PPP moving forward will be prepared. At current stage, MPWT is in the process of preparing new project, Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance Project, using one of PPP concept as Output and Performance-Based Road Contract (OPBRC).

B.1.b Advisory services for provincial and rural management: Maintenance monitoring consultant has been recruited for day-to-day monitoring of provincial periodic maintenance and spot improvements. B.1.c ICT development: The design and development of ICT tools to support road asset management, Integrated Road Asset Management System (IRAM or system), is completed and testing was performed in June – July 2015. ICT Steering Committee has reviewed and approved the IRAM. Training for users was conducted in February 2016 and the system has been officially operated in May 2016. Procurements of ICT equipment for two packages have been completed and payments were fully made to the contractors. B.1.d URMF data collection: Annual Road Asset Report for FY 14/15 was submitted to DoR, DPC and WB in November 2015. The condition survey for national roads for FY 15/16 including data collection, with limited budget of USD20 thousand, was completed in March 2016 and its analysis has been completed in May 2016. Data input, validation and analysis of road condition for local roads was completed and Annual Road Asset Report for FY 15/16 was issued in March 2017. B.1.f Fiduciary support: At the first stage of the Project, this role was under DPC and later under DoF since it was established in 2013.

MPWT together with WB developed the Internal Financial Manual of MPWT which was approved by Minister in 2010 and revision was made in September 2017 (including Standard Operating Procedures) by assisting of National Coordination and FM Page 12 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report Consultants. New version of APACC (and accounting software) was upgraded and used as the Project software in recording financial information and generating financial reports such Interim Financial Reports (IFRs), financial statements and etc. At the first year of Project implementation, there were poor quality and delays submission of the IFRs and Project audit reports. The quality of the IFRs and timing of submission of both IFRs and audit reports continued to improve after the second year of implementation. The audit opinions were unqualified (clean) throughout Project implementation. From June 2015, the Project recruited a National Coordination Adviser and three Financial Management Advisers to advise the Project in coordination and financial management including revision of Internal Financial Manual. As all of the staffs working on the financial management of the Project were staffs of MPWT and DPWT, the Project was instrumental in improving the overall capacity of ministry and provincial staffs to manage the finances of ODA projects.

4.2.2 ESOM B.2.a ESOM preparation: PTI has finished its translation of ESOM to English version and already submitted to the Bank for comments in early October 2015. Upon receiving comments from the Bank, PTI will revise and collaborate with the Council of Science and Technology in preparation to seek the minister’s approval on the revised ESOM. However, The Bank will review the ESOM in parallel with safeguard preparation for the new project to ensure consistency. As recommended by the Bank, ESD/PTI and TED/DOR completed submission work plan on E&S monitoring for provincial road maintenance to the Bank. However, it was cancel due to the WB keep priority to the preparation safeguards framework for LRSP 2 (ESMF, RPF, EGPF) which is urgent needed to submit to head quarter. B.2.b Environment, social and safeguard monitoring: The E&S monitoring (completion report) of NR1B and NR6A, and of provincial road maintenance have been completed. Random visit to verify the safeguard compliance for the provincial road maintenance projects of five Northern provinces (Xayabuly, Bokeo, Luangnamtha, Oudomxay and Phongsaly) during 21-30 December 2015 with no major issues were noticed. PTI also completed safeguard training in Laung Prabang for 8 DPWTs in January 2016.

ESD/PTI conducted several consultation for preparing safeguards framework for LRSP 2 such as: i) the first consultation was made in Vientiane on 25 February 2016 to inform the public and key agencies about the objective and scope of the Project as well as the draft TORs for the ESMF, RPF, and EGPF while the second consultant was made in Vientiane on 29 April 2016 on the draft ESMF, RPF, and EGPF; ii) two consultations were also made in the Bolikhamxay and Xayabuly. The first consultation in BKX and XBL were made in 04 to 11 of March 2016 to describe scope of the subprojects to be carried out in the provinces, consult the draft TORs for ESMF, and RPF as well as collect baseline data to identify if ethnic groups are present in the subproject areas and/or possible effected people and/or property that may be affected by the subprojects; iii) the second consultation which was conducted in XBL during 20-23 April 2016 and in BKX in 25-27 April 2016. Results for the second consultation confirmed strong support for the project as well as the ESMF, RPF, and EGPF to be applied to the Project; and iv) additional consultation has conducted for concerned provincial departments in Houaphan and Oudomxay during 28 June and 9 July 2016.

4.2.3 Internal controls Page 13 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report B.3.a Advisory services and training for internal control division: Financial audit manual, financial audit working papers, technical audit manual, technical audit working papers, quality assurance guidance, strategy for internal auditing plan, and strategy for financial management system in English, which produced by Nanjing Audit University, have been completely translated into Lao language while the first workshop has been conducted on 15-19 August 2016 for gathering comments from nationwide inspectors of MPWT (by using GoL’s budget) and second was made in December 2016 for 9 northern provinces while for 9 southern provinces was made in January 2017. DoI completed its procurement for equipment and vehicles to six provinces in August 2015 and distribution to those provinces were also completed. A national coordination advisor and three financial management advisors have been on board since June 2015 while another two internal control consultants are now postponed and recruited under new project (Lao Road Sector Project 2). All internal control weaknesses identified by Ernst & Young in Internal Control Assessment Report dated 21 December 2012 and certain internal control weaknesses that highlighted in the Management Letter for the year ended 30 September 2014 by EY have been fully implemented.

B.3.b Technical audit: The consultant for technical audit of NR6A, NR1B and provincial roads has been on board since May 2015. The consultant has been completed his technical audit report in September 2015. During the nationwide workshop for inspection sectors, which held in September 2015 at Vangvieng of Vientiane Province, the Consultant completed his introduction to Quality Assurance and Control. B.3.c Financial audit: Ernst & Young Lao Co., Ltd is the external auditor for the whole period of the Project. Although certain delays in submission of audited reports, however, the audit opinions were unqualified (clean) throughout Project implementation. The final audit was carried out in January 2018 and now is process of signing and the audited reports will be submitted to World Bank in March 2018. B.3.d Capacity building: Nationwide workshop for inspection sectors was held in September 2015 at Vangvieng of Vientiane Province with approximated 100 participants to introduce new Prime Minister Decree PM01/PM dated 6 January 2015 mandates the internal control division of the relevant department at central and provincial level to review all new contracts before these are signed.

First workshop, (on Financial audit manual, financial audit working papers, technical audit manual, technical audit working papers, quality assurance guidance, strategy for internal auditing plan, and strategy for financial management system), has been conducted on 15-19 August 2016 for gathering comments from nationwide inspectors of MPWT (by using GoL’s budget) and second was made in December 2016 for 9 northern provinces while for 9 southern provinces was made in January 2017. 4.2.4 Provincial capacity development: The capacity development plans were focused on enhancing ministerial, provincial and district capacities for equality control, financial and contract management. Total 2,042 participants (286 females and 1,756 males) including 727 participants from Ministry, 1,089 from provinces and 226 from districts were trained during the Project period. Page 14 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report 4.3 Disaster Recovery and Contingency: It has been agreed in a follow-up meeting on Agreed Actions that DOR with a support from DOF and DPC will draft the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for the management of the emergency contingency fund. The third drafted SOP for the Emergency Response and Disaster Recovery Fund has been reviewed and commented by DoR and DoR who agreed in principles on the fund allocation, scope of the use and activation procedures.

Final draft has been completed and attached to the Internal Financial Manual which approved by Minister on 8 September 2017. 5. Scorings: Highly satisfactory > 2.7; satisfactory 2.7>S>1.6; partly satisfactory 1.6>PS>0.8; unsatisfactory<0.8.

The performance of the Bank and Borrower were based upon the above criteria. 6.1 Bank’s Performance Relevance – in continuation of the institutional outcomes achieved from previous operations, especially the Bank-led, multi-donor funded Road Maintenance Program Phase 1 and 2, and add value through financing crucial physical investment, and supporting the strategic planning, design, preparation, implementation, and management of road infrastructure in an environmentally and socially responsible manner. ECONOMIC ASPECTS The Project is fully consistent with the World Bank’s Country Assistance Strategy (CAS) for Lao PDR.

It supports one of the main CAS pillars of sustained growth through enhanced regional integration and private sector development, and to a lesser extent, one of the supporting CAS Page 22 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report objectives regarding better alignment of donor resources with the objectives of the Government’s National Growth and Poverty Eradication Strategy and strengthened aid coordination. The improved road services for national roads impacted low-income households in Phongsaly province (Khua, Boonneua, and Boontai Districts) and Huaphan province (Xienkhor, Sopbao, and Add Districts). Most of them, based on the location, are low-income households in rural areas. The provincial road maintenance was implemented country-wide and has impact on the rural population, which is more than 2/3 of the total population. Because most of provincial roads are unpaved and vulnerable to flood and landslides, road maintenance is crucial in ensuring all year round accessibility, which provides access to employment, market, school, and health services. The Project’s benefits have been distributed more to lower-income population, as well as shared among all provinces in Lao PDR.

The Project directly supports the economic growth as following: ➢ In line with these objectives, the Project supports the country’s economic growth and poverty reduction through: (i) reducing road transport costs for goods and passengers; (ii) rehabilitating the road damaged by Typhoon Ketsana; and (iii) developing an emergency contingency fund for rapid response to natural disasters in the road sector. Support to the second CAS objective is mainly through the strengthening of the MPWT’s systems for strategic planning, fiduciary management, and environmental safeguards, which are required for achieving better aid harmonization and coordination; ➢ At appraisal, the travel times on NR 6A (62km) and NR 1B (109km) were 3 hours and 5 hours, respectively. The target was to reduce travel time by 40%. ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL ASPECTS Environmental Safeguards: Safeguard compliance is considered Satisfactory based on the documents provided, discussions with the Project stakeholders, and field visits to NR1B and NR6A and some provincial roads in Phongsaly, Oudomxay, Houaphan and Xiengkhouang. No major safeguards related issues were Page 23 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report identified and reported during Project implementation. All required written evidence was made available for the mission’s review when required. The quality of safeguard documentation could be further improved with advanced training, and support will be provided to MPWT and the DPWTs under LRSP2. Safeguard monitoring of NR 6A and 1B and Provincial Road Maintenance: Civil works for NR 1B and NR 6A and provincial road maintenance were completed with no major safeguards concerns.

The mission noted that the Project contributed significantly to dust reduction in communities where roads were upgraded from unpaved to paved standard. The PTRI had conducted periodic Environment and Social (E&S) monitoring, including final E&S monitoring during December 22 –30, 2015 on road NR1B in Phongsaly and six sub-projects of provincial road maintenance in five northern provinces (Xayabouly, Borkeo, Luangnamtha, Oudomxay and Phongsaly). Common issues found by the mission include: improper use and poor management of borrow pits, improper camp site management (waste management, use of materials from natural resources, etc.), inadequate warning sign installation, soil erosion, poor construction waste disposal, etc. These issues had been considered and included in the design of LRSP2, particularly with respect to implementation and enforcement of safeguards obligations in contractor contracts and contractor management and capacity building. All safeguards trainings planned for LRSP have been completed. The mission also discussed with the DPWTs the way forward for LRSP2. Environment and Social Operations Manual (ESOM) updates and implementation. In 2015 PTRI had finished the ESOM updates to include new regulations and had finished an English translation. The English version was submitted to the Bank for review in October 2015, but was found by the Bank to require further improvement.

However, since the Department of Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (DESIA) of the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE) plans to upgrade the Environment and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) and Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) regulations into ESIA law or decree in 2017–2018, and LRSP2 will include TA support to prepare several guidelines on safeguards in road sector investment projects, the mission suggested that the ESOM updates be continued and included under LRSP2 implementation. Preparation of PPP NR13 Road Project: The Feasibility Study (FS) for the PPP for NR 13N and 13S has been completed, but the Environmental and Social (E&S) Assessment was found insufficient for a World Bank Group (WBG) financed Category A project. Procurement of an additional E&S study is in process. At the same time, MPWT informed the mission that due to the current economic and financial situation, the government is not in favor of the implementing a PPP project as proposed for NR 13 N and 13 S road sections and had decided to terminate the Financial Advisory Services Agreement with the IFC for the PPP road project. However, MPWT still seeks IDA support for NR 13N improvement. Investment on NR 13S is still in GoL’s plan, but would be carried out in a later phase. With this decision and partly because of cost and financing implications, the E&S study of NR 13N and NR 13S will now be conducted separately.

The proposed first step will be to carry out additional planning activities and update the ESIA, Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) and Ethnic Group Development Plan (EGDP) for the 13N road section only. The MPWT has revised the E&S TORs to reflect this split and clearly describe coverage of each contract and its interface. The International Environmental Specialist contract for the E&S study of NR 13N and 13S, which ended Page 24 of 25 LRSP – Implementation Completion Report in November 2016, will be revised and renewed for only the NR 13N road section. As discussed in para 26 under Procurement for the E&S Study, MPWT has received the revised technical and financial proposals from the firm whose scope of work would now include all safeguards surveys and preparation of social safeguards instruments including the RAP and EGDP. The mission discussed that these factors - the need for more time for study completion than remains under LRSP, a higher cost estimate than the available budget, and the requirement to incorporate preparation of a full RAP – all suggest that the study would best be carried out under LRSP2. Social Safeguard: Safeguard monitoring of NR 6A and NR 1B and Provincial Road Maintenance. On the basis of the safeguard monitoring, RAP completion reports reviewed, and field visit to NR 6A and some provincial roads in Xiengkhouang conducted during the mission, no major issue was identified.

The RAP implementation has been completed with compensation and required support provided to all Project Affected Households (PAH). All written evidence, including minutes of consultation meetings, receipts and agreements, were made available for review. The PAHs met confirmed the receipt of cash compensation from the Project and expressed their appreciation for the improved roads and positive impacts on their livelihood. There were some grievances expressed mainly related to the need for further improvement of road safety measures such as traffic control sign posts at some points of the NR6A. The quality of safeguard documentation could be further improved with advanced training, updated templates and samples of comprehensive RAPs and reports to be provided for the MPWT and the DPWTs for their references under the LRSP2. 9. LESSONS LEARNED Straightforward project design supported easy adjustments during the life of the project. Clear, not overly ambitious targets were set and sufficiently straightforward to be easily adjusted when required. The Project design provided a clear line-of-sight from outputs to objectives, which made it possible for the project to be easily adapted to unexpected challenges. The use of long-term improvement and maintenance contracts can help improve road asset management and enhance sector efficiencies. Climate resilient road designs are critical and need to be promoted to reduce infrastructure vulnerability to current and future climate risk.

No Components Table Name Component A: Road Asset Management System (RAMS) Development:(Cost $10.00 M) Component B: Road Asset Preservation:(Cost $156.60 M) Component C: Road Asset Improvement:(Cost $133.40 M) Component D: Institutional Strengthening Program:(Cost $1.70 M) Overall Ratings Name Previous Rating Current Rating Progress towards achievement of PDO Satisfactory Satisfactory Overall Implementation Progress (IP) Satisfactory Moderately Satisfactory Overall Risk Rating Low Low Implementation Status and Key Decisions The project was approved by the Board on December 12, 2013 with the Financing Agreement signed on January 14, 2014 and became effective on April 11, 2014. Overall, the project implementation has progressed well with satisfactory completion of all components as originally planned. All PDO and intermediate indicators have fully achieved or overachieved their targets. For the original scope, contracts for goods, works and services have been completed successfully. The Road Asset Management System (RAMS) has been developed and is fully operational to effectively enhance the preparation of the medium term investment plan (MTIP) for 2021-2025 as well as prioritization of the maintenance plan for the whole national highway network in a sustainable and transparent approach. The institutional strengthening program was satisfactorily completed, too.

The implementation of the first additional activities (using US$31.98 million) for improvement of NH6 in Son La and NH2 in Ha Giang. All seven civil works contracts have been progressing very well and are on track for completion by the current project closing date of December 31, 9/11/2022 Page 1 of 7 The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) 2022. Land acquisition and resettlement (LAR) activities which started in early 2020 have reached 98 percentage completion for NH6 and 99 percentage completion for NH2. Implementation of the second additional activity for NH9 improvement (using US$21.64 million) has been seriously delayed. The consultants for construction supervision, safeguards monitoring and financial audit have been mobilized since March 2022. Two civil works contracts of about US$9 million were signed in March and construction has started from March 31, 2022. However, the LAR activities which are funded/implemented by Quang Tri province have been seriously delayed. So far, only 4.5 km of land from either side of the road have been cleared. The main cause of this delay is the low estimates for the total LAR costs of VND 75 billions evaluated in 2020 compared to the current market cost of VND 345 billion. The Provincial People’s Committee (PPC) is only able to allocate VND75 billion for LAR activities by July 2022. The remaining VND 270 billion has been recently secured in August 2022.

However, it is very unlikely that the LAR activities could be completed and handed over by September 2022 to allow adequate time for works to be constructed with acceptable quality. This is putting in jeopardy the implementation of the NH9 improvement. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL Context 1. At the time of project appraisal, Viet Nam was enjoying a period of rapid economic growth and livelihoods had improved greatly. Real gross domestic product (GDP) had increased at an average annual rate of 7.4 percent between 1990 and 2010, placing the country among the top five globally for growth over that period. In fact, between 1993 and 2014, Viet Nam's amazing rise from a low-income to middle-income position pulled 40 million people out of poverty; in other words, the proportion of people living in poverty fell from 60 percent in 1993 to 14 percent in 2014.1 Nevertheless, rural households with limited access to economic development and opportunities remained at risk of extreme poverty, and they were the targeted beneficiaries of this project. 2. Viet Nam's development trajectory was significantly influenced by infrastructure investment.

Annual infrastructure spending was maintained at between nine and 10 percent of GDP, with transport accounting for nearly half of this amount over the same period (1990 to 2010). As urbanization continued to spread (it was anticipated that by 2020, about 50 percent of the Vietnamese population would live in urban areas), further expansion of the road, rail, and inland waterway transport networks was necessary to relieve bottlenecks, improve productivity, and meet important growth and poverty reduction targets. Sectoral context 3. Viet Nam’s road transport network has improved over the past decades. At appraisal, the overall length of the entire road network in Viet Nam was approximately 210,000 km, of which 17,199 km were national highways, and 17,450 km were provincial roads. The bulk of the 131,951 km (about 63 percent) comprised rural roads. The density of the road network was 677 km per 1,000 km2 and 2.41 km per 1,000 people. Although the network had grown, 30 percent of Viet Nam's national highways were still in "poor" or "very poor" condition. Overall, only roughly half of the road network was paved. 4. The Government of Viet Nam (GoV) invested in transport infrastructure. It recognized that to address sectoral challenges and maintain current road conditions, the allocation of financing to strengthen infrastructure would be crucial.

Analysis in 2012 showed that preservation of the existing state of the country’s roads (routine/periodic maintenance and rehabilitation) would cost US$ 360 million per year. The government adopted a strategy to increase recurrent expenditure on road maintenance. Through the creation of a Road Maintenance Fund (RMF), the GoV expected to increase revenue streams for road maintenance, and therefore asked the World Bank for assistance to finance upgrading of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS) to improve planning of regular maintenance and upgrading of strategically chosen corridors of the National Highway (NH) network. 6. The Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (VRAMP) was designed to contribute cutting-edge thinking on planning and prioritization of road maintenance for sustainability. VRAMP is based on the World Bank’s engagement with the GoV and lessons learned from Road Network Improvement Project (RNIP) P059663 (US$ 225.26 million) which supported an efficient transport network and preservation of existing assets.

VRAMP supported the Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) FY12–FY16 Pillar 1: strengthening Viet Nam's competitiveness in the regional and global economy through improved quality and efficiency of infrastructure services aimed at reduced travel times on targeted transport corridors. The project also supported Pillar 3: expanding opportunities by reducing inequality for ethnic minorities. The project continues to be relevant to Focus Area 1 (Objective 3) of the current World Bank strategy for Viet Nam: enhance trade competitiveness, multi-modal transport connectivity, and logistics services (CPF for FY18–FY22).2 All of these aspects sought to strengthen economic growth and provide opportunities for the project beneficiaries. Theory of Change (Results Chain) 7. A theory of change (ToC) was not required at the time of project appraisal.

Figure 1 showed the retrospective ToC developed by the Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) team based on the project development objective (PDO), project description, and Results Framework.3 The restructuring in December 2020 did not affect the ToC, and it sought to address issues of (i) inadequate planning for road maintenance due to insufficient data on road condition—this aligns with PDO section on ‘improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national road asset management’; (ii) use of relatively costly traditional contractual arrangements for road—this aligns with the PDO section on ‘sustainability of maintenance practices’; and (iii) formally framing as an outcome the reduced travel times resulting from improved road surfaces, especially along the roads maintained under the Project. 8. The long-term outcome in the project areas was to improve the efficiency and sustainability of road asset management and improve the efficiency and sustainability of road maintenance practices. This aims to improve connectivity and economic activities for the communities along the road corridors and across regional borders. To achieve this long-term objective would require increasing the use of the road asset management database to plan and prioritize transport connectivity on the national network, preserve infrastructural assets, increase accessibility to roads and bridges, strengthen capacity for management of PBCs, and finance road infrastructure.

The project development objective is to improve the efficiency and sustainability of the road asset management and maintenance practices performed by the Ministry of Transport (MOT) on national roads in Viet Nam.4 Key Expected Outcomes and Outcome Indicators 10. The project has been designed to achieve the PDO through a two-pronged approach: PDO outcome 1: Improving efficiency and sustainability of Road Asset Management Practices. This is to be achieved through Component A (establishment of RAMs, increasing financing for road maintenance, introduction of PBC contracts including through developing enabling legal framework, and so forth) and Component D (institutional strengthening, capacity building, and so forth). The achievements are to be measured through the following outcome/output indicators: • Roads rehabilitated in good or fair condition as a share of total classified roads.

SIGNIFICANT CHANGES DURING IMPLEMENTATION (IF APPLICABLE) 12. A level two restructuring was approved in December 2020 to scale up and extend the closing date of the project by 24 months, up to December 31, 2022. The project benefited from savings in the amount of US$ 55.07 million due to the competitive procurement processes and the GoV still provided its counterpart financing notwithstanding the savings. Additional activities introduced into the project included: (i) pavement (road surface) strengthening and intersections of 7.7 km section of NH6 under component B; (ii) construction of a 19.5 km bypass in Son La city under NH2; (iii) improvement and expansion of 1.39 km NH2 under Component C.

These changes introduced during project implementation were beneficial, with output directly linked to the PDO. 13. Additional cost savings in the amount of US$ 21.64 million from procurement processes led to including under the project activities the rehabilitation of NH9 (13.9 km) without a formal restructuring or amendment to the Financing Agreement. The addition of NH9’s 13.8 km road section from Cua Viet port to NH1. This additional activity was requested from the GoV and agreed by the Bank. A decision was reached not to amend the FA to finance this work because the legal agreement was flexible in its language. Rehabilitation of NH9 was not implemented and by Project closing the unused funds for this activity were refunded to the Bank and the scope of work was cancelled from the project and all contracts related to NH9 (including construction, supervision) were terminated except the design contract was completed. Revised PDO Indicators and Outcome Targets 14. The PDO indicators were not formally revised. Some targets were included in the scale-up—a total of 20.89 km of roads added to NH6 (19.5 km), and NH2 (1.39 km). The results framework targets were revised to include the additional roads and they were monitored during project implementation (see Annex 1). RELEVANCE OF PDOs 17. The project objective is aligned with the World Bank Group Country Partnership Framework (CPF) FY18 –22.5 The PDO is still a development priority and issue relevant to Objective 2 of the CPF’s Focus Area 1, ‘Promoting private sector and agri-business development’; and Focus Area 3, 'Enhance trade competitiveness and multi-modal transport connectivity and logistics services in Viet Nam’. To improve the efficiency and sustainability of road asset management, RAMS has been developed: a successful and well-functioning platform which produced accurate information on road asset management. To enhance data integrity, security, data entry accuracy and operational effectiveness, DRVN and PMU staff capacity were enhanced. The project financed data collection equipment including vehicles and customized software for collecting data on the NHs network and analysis by professionals for decision-making. The system utilizes a cloud computing platform to combine and share data from various existing systems, such as the Pavement Management System (PMS) funded by JICA, and the Bridge Management System (VBMS) funded by DRVN. The centralized system supported the nationwide rollout of the new system to monitor and analyze conditions on the NH road network.

At inception, to establish the database, 1,148 items of data were broken down into general information, statistics, inspection, repair history, and property value. The centralized system also added data on 33 different NH assets of the NH network and their attributes, such as road surface conditions and bridges, over several years in order of priority for maintenance planning to ensure the sustainability and preservation of the structural Page 11 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) integrity of Viet Nam’s national highway network.8 This allowed for efficiency and transparency in planning, annual budget allocation, the prioritization of investment, and maintenance of the national road network. 24. RAMS is connected to the public road network assets system managed by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and has created unit costs and cost norms for maintenance and management. During the project implementation, DRVN issued regulations on management, operation, and exploration of RAMS. The system provides information for continued piloting of maintenance planning for roads, bridges and 32 other assets for some routes under Regional Road Management Bureaus (RRMBs).

Given the excellent performance of RAMS, at the time of closing the system is the nationwide method used for evaluating pavement conditions—and more importantly, this has meant that DRVN and Provincial Departments of Transport (PDoTs) across the country have been able to access data on road conditions for planning and budgeting. 25. Expansion of PBC program in national road maintenance. PBC contracts are quite new in Viet Nam compared to the traditional method of road maintenance. Over the past 20 years prior to the project, the government has tried to introduce the PBC model with little success. VRAMP succeeded in piloting a PBC roll out. The groundwork involved establishing the regulatory system for PBC contracts (including regulatory framework, standard bidding documents and PBC supervision manual, plus training to build the institutional capacity of relevant agencies and contractors) and research to compare the effectiveness of different maintenance methods to ensure effective implementation. The project financed and implemented 234 km of roads under PBC maintenance contracts for NH6 for 48 months and for NH2 for 60 months. Based on the successful results of PBC maintenance in the project, DRVN has expanded the PBC model for the maintenance of whole National Highway network. 26. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 47. Project objective and strategic direction. The objectives of VRAMP were highly relevant, given the challenges facing Viet Nam in terms of managing road assets. The project was a follow-on to the (now closed) RNIP and drew lessons from it on the importance of improved maintenance practices. MOT, DRVN and PMU3’s capacity was enhanced to manage PBCs and the national road network, and to establish the Road Asset Management Framework through a study tour on PBCs (to Brazil) and on PPP (to India, China, and Malaysia). The selection of priority sites and bridges was based on sound criteria. The initial sequencing of tasks and timing was appropriate, as it focused on PBCs and the maintenance of networks for better connectivity from the provinces to urban centers. The procurement processes ensured 30 percent of bidding documents were prepared and available by project negotiations. The project had a high level of readiness for implementation, after Board approval. Page 19 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) 49. Implementation arrangement. The World Bank conducted an internal appraisal process and confirmed that the additional work was feasible and that it was justifiable to finance NH9 improvement under VRAMP within the 16-month period left for implementation.

This was admittedly ambitious, but consideration was given because (i) Quang Tri province had been performing very well to implement WB projects over the prior 20 years (that is, RTP1, 2, 3 and LRAMP); (ii) Quang Tri’s LAR was relatively small and uncomplicated, compared with the one from Son La province, where LAR and construction were completed within two years. Quang Tri failed to execute the LARs due to the increased cost of LAR (a five-fold increase) even though MOT/DRVN/PMU3 put in an extraordinary effort to accelerate the bidding and launch of works and consultant contracts within eight months of the Project Investment Plan (PIP) being approved for NH9. However, MOT’s efforts were jeopardized by LAR failure and Quang Tri province underestimating the cost of LAR at the time of this ICR. BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME A. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) M&E Design 61. DRVN and PMU3 were responsible for monitoring results and activities. A dedicated M&E unit in DRVN, PMU3, the Supervision consultant and designated staff in the provinces contributed to ensuring data availability and collection at all levels of implementation. The Project procured modern road surface condition data collection devices which were compatible with the PMS system and supported DRVN with data collection and processing of images obtained from CCTV cameras, surface crack detection using the international roughness index (IRI), road surface settlement, surveys, and geographic coordinates. The overall results framework was appropriate for measuring the achievements of the project outcomes and outputs. The linkage between the intermediate results indicators and the PDO outcomes was measurable. However, some indicators were not attributable to the project. The PDO indicators on Roads Rehabilitated targets were not attributable to the project and therefore cannot serve to verify that the entire NH Network has been rehabilitated during the project, over and above measuring the conditions of the network and action plan for rehabilitation. This project built on and expanded support from previous World Bank financed projects in Viet Nam in an area that remains relevant and strategic to the country’s efforts to improve connectivity from the national level to the provinces. Infrastructure development through the improvement and maintenance of the existing national road network is key to achieving sustainable and inclusive development. The project supported Viet Nam at a critical time when other donors, including the ADB and JICA, sought to strengthen RAMS through the development of software as a tool for the analysis of preservation options, planning and direct investment in infrastructure maintenance. The use of PBCs (which were relatively new in Viet Nam at the time) optimized the process of road asset management, resulting in increased usage of PBCs, coupled with training, specialized capacity development, and ownership by MOT, DRVN, PMU3, and the provinces. 76. GoV support to the established RAMS. Broadly speaking, the GoV’s efforts to preserve the RAMS have a high likelihood of continued expansion on the achievement of the PDO. The RAMS, if used effectively, is expected to produce reliable data that will enhance GoV decisions regarding the maintenance of the NH corridors constructed under the project and beyond. The RAMS/RAMF are updated by staff (who received RAMS training and certificate) from DRVN and PDoTs. DRVN had faced financial difficulties in maintaining the virtual servers and Wi-Fi services but has allocated its own budget while waiting for official allocation from MOT. Capacity already built within DRVN/PMU3 on PBC is to be sustained. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 83. Ownership, support, and leadership at the National and Provincial level were critical to success. At the National level, there was sustained ownership under the leadership of the Ministry of Transportation (MOT) and strong leadership by DRVN and PMU3, the implementing agency. This ensured continued growth in financing to accommodate the project needs. These efforts need to be sustained. At the provincial level, there was strong support for and Page 27 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) understanding of the project by PPCs, who engaged regularly with key local stakeholders and beneficiaries in relation to resettlement and road sections within their jurisdiction. This resulted in successful completion of activities. These committees should be strengthened and their experiences showcased as those of exemplary results-oriented achievers. The structures and relationships formed in the districts—as well as the local leadership—were fundamental to the success of the project. 84. Sustainability and institutionalization of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS). The establishment of the RAMS is a positive impact to maintain sustainability of transport assets in Viet Nam and a global example of planning for road maintenance. Through technological advances, the new system with its unique software produced timely data conducive to reliable responses in upgrading of the road network.

One of the most significant achievements of RAMS is an effective planning tool linked to the government’s existing road and asset management systems that brings together relevant National Highways and Provincial roads data. The road management agencies are empowered to generate periodic data reports, planning for maintenance, and upgrading of the road network. The innovations and transparent operations of RAMS have evolved to become one of the largest data collection systems in Viet Nam. As a result, the RAMS model has been adopted by other Ministries for issuance of driver’s licenses, and monitoring trucking overload, among other purposes. 85. PBCs are crucial for successful implementation and sustainability of road maintenance. The 234km maintained by the project under the PBC method along NH 2 and NH 6 effected a move away from traditional road construction. This was key for maintaining excellent road surface, traffic safety and drainage, allowing for smooth and steady traffic for five years after the contracts had expired. Exposure to global practices aimed at sustaining technical skills on the concepts of PBC proved vital for promoting long-term maintenance of high-quality roads in the future. At the policy level, following the results of this robust innovation, PBC is being decentralized and expanded across Viet Nam for the maintenance and repair of National Highways. 86.

Efficient and timely payment of compensation for resettlement and land acquisition is critical for project implementation. Delays in resettlement are a systemic challenge encountered in the Viet Nam country portfolio. The World Bank and the GoV are working to address these issues. Under the project, land acquisition and resettlement ended up requiring five times more than the original budget allocation. Current market prices and land price increases had not been foreseen, and implementation delays were the consequence. This project's experience has demonstrated the need to closely monitor and prepare for price adjustment scale during implementation and request the appropriate allocation as needed. A land price agreement and prompt payment of compensation would lessen the effects of rising land prices and implementation delays. 87. Adding new activities to a well-performing project should be carefully analyzed, especially given a long LAR implementation period. In the context of this project, the additional activities were ambitious considering the capacity of the implementing agency, the financial constraints of the PPC, and time left for implementation without extension. When discussing additional activities, in-depth assessment, selectivity, clearly defined activities with timeline and risk mitigation measures should be factored in to provide a clear view of what is possible to be accomplished within the time left before project closing. .

Key achievements to date include the rehabilitation of the entire Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border road (Suakoko Highway). The rehabilitation of the rural section was completed in 2016 and is under the long-term maintenance phases under the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The travel time along the road has reduced by 50% and the road remains in overall good physical condition, and the levels of service are largely achieved. A Multi-Modal Transport Plan (including a Strategic Investment Plan) has been formulated and 915 RAP entitlements have also been fully paid with IDA funding under the project. Under Road Safety Component, the following has also been achieved (i) Road safety schoolbooks (125,000No.) printed, (ii) Streets Naming, Traffic Warning & County Welcome Signs installed, (iii) Training undertaken for truck drivers commercial and motorcycle and (iv) communications (toll free number 5888) for emergency response system for post-crash response operational; (v) Road marking completed for 15km out of 62km of streets in Monrovia; (vi) speed guns and breathalyzers procured for Liberia National Police (LNP) and training in various aspects of road safety carried out for a total of 1,109 staff across agencies, including 693 women (62%). The government has communicated its decision on the counterpart funding for the OPRC Lots 1 and 2, essentially rescheduling its counterpart funding contribution to the project over the next three budget years.

The project is currently being restructured to reflect this change in the funding arrangements. The Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border road (Suakoko Highway), rehabilitation of which was completed in 2016, is under the long-term maintenance phases under the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The first 2.1km length between Red Light and Coca Cola Junction was completed in March 2020. The remaining 4km section was handed over to the Contracting Entity in December 2020 and is progressing steadily. The target is to complete the major works activities by June 2022. The slow pace of road sector reforms continues to be a significant risk to sustainability of Liberia’s road sector. While the Road Sector Development Partners Platform has been reactivated to discuss road sector issues, the Bank is providing Technical Assistance to the Ministry of Public Works for the preparation of a proposed 10-year Road Sector Development Plan. The RSDP will be a government-led, collaborative, and comprehensive planning process with broad stakeholder engagement to refocus the strategic direction of the sector. This will stimulate further discussion and progress on institutional reforms.

The Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border road (Suakoko Highway) is under a long term maintenance phase of the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The road sector reform agenda has made little progress. The National Road Fund recently established is facing challenges in receiving the required transfers of the fuel levy, and steps need to be taken by GOL to address the irregular and inadequate transfers to ensure sustainability of the sector investments. Government action is also needed on the draft the Road Act and Road Agency Act which are critical pillars of the road reforms to consolidate the gains in the sector over the past years.

The project is on course to achieve all its targets and indicators. The additional financing (US$40 million) approved in May 2017 was declared effective January 24, 2018. Suakoko Highway is under a long term maintenance phase of the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The road, which extends from Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border, remains in overall good physical condition. The road sector reform has slowed recently.

However, some progress is made regarding the road fund. A road fund manager is appointed and the Government is in the process of setting up road fund accounts. There is a legal challenge against collection of fuel levy by the road fund. The Supreme Court has stayed the collection of road fund levy following the legal challenge. The issue is yet to be resolved. However, the Supreme Court decision is expected in June 2018. The Highway Act and Road Agency Act are prepared. They are expected to be taken up by the new Legislature soon. The implementation of the rehabilitation of the ELWA Junction to Red Light Road section (6.5km), planned to commence by March 2018, is delayed. The Government needs to make some revisions to the resettlement action plan and to initiate resettlement activities. The Bank is currently discussing the way forward with the government.

Despite the progress to date, the Government of Liberia's fiscal constraints pose a long-term risk to the sustainability of the project's outcomes and the government has sought additional financing from IDA of US$40 million to i) reduce its counterpart contributions to the project; ii) cover a financing shortfall arising from site handover delays and Ebola-related force majeure; iii) finance road safety and right of way preservation measures; and iv) and finance resettlement along the remaining section of the corridor which is pending rehabilitation (ELWA junction to Red Light). The Technical Support Group (TSG) services are progressing satisfactorily and the Multi Modal Transport Study is expected to conclude as per the plan (end June 2017). The Government is yet to resolve outstanding claims.

The Government and the Lot 2 contractor have finalized a variation order related to site handover delays and force majeure. A similar claim for the Lot 1 contractor is under negotiation. Rehabilitation of the LIBRAMP corridor (248 km) is completed, a dedication ceremony was held in October 2016, and the road has been renamed Suakoko Highway. Lot 1 (178 km) entered the maintenance phase in September 2016, while Lot 2 did so in March. Despite physical progress, cost overruns and exchange rate losses mean LIBRAMP will require additional financial resources. The government has also been unable to contribute the promised counterpart financing (US$72.8 million over ten years). The government is considering various options to mitigate the situation and project risk, such as requesting additional financing or dropping some pending activities, and a response is pending.

A public employee has admitted responsibility for theft of five missing RAP payments checks. Restitution has been received for one check, leaving an ineligible expenditure balance of US$11,348. Unless further restitution is paid, the World Bank will request the ineligible expenditure be returned by the Government of Liberia (GoL). Residents in some areas have raised concern about impacts of road construction equipment vibration on their homes. The IIU has been asked to ensure an appropriate and accessible project Grievance Redress Mechanism is triggered to follow up on all claims of property damage under the project. As mentioned in the previous ISR sequence, the improvement in pavement condition has led to increased traffic speeds and had a negative impact on road safety in the short term. A partial road safety assessment had identified national-level and corridor-level road safety deficiencies The Monitoring Consultant for Lots 1 has been tasked to submit report on road safety along the corridor by end November 2016. The Infrastructure Implementation Unit of the Ministry of Public Works and the Government have yet to resolve outstanding contractual issues. Variation orders to account for Ebola-related force majeure and delayed site handover are yet to be finalized for the Lot 1 works contract. Refund of previously levied import taxes (due to change in regulations) is still pending US$1.3 million.

The government has agreed to clarify procedures for this reimbursement process but has so far not done so. The Lot 1 Contractor is owed an additional US$490,000 for explosive import costs due to new government regulations. The services for preparing the concept design and bidding documents for ELWA Junction-Red Light intersection -Coca Cola Factory road section are ongoing. Physical progress of the major road works, Red Light to Gbarnga and Gbarnga to Ganta/Guinea Border, is well advanced. The segment from Gbarnga to Guinea Border was declared completed and dedicated in March 2016. The Monrovia-Gbarnga road segment is more than 80 percent completed. The Government of Liberia has committed to resolve a few outstanding resettlement compensation cases end of April of 2016. The Government is also investigating into allegations of wrongdoing in RAP payments and a formal report is due by May 16, 2016. As mentioned in the previous ISR sequence, the improvement in pavement condition has led to increased traffic speeds and had a negative impact on road safety in the short term.

A partial road safety assessment identified national-level and corridor-level road safety deficiencies and the results have been shared with the Government of Liberia, but corridor road safety studies by the monitoring consultants are past due. Infrastructure Implementation Unit of the Ministry of Public Works shall endeavor to resolve outstanding contractual issues. Variation orders to account for Ebola-related force majeure and delayed site handover are yet to be finalized for the two corridor works contracts but cost increases are likely to be significant. Refund of previously levied import taxes (due to change in regulations) is still pending and has accrued to be US$1.3 million. The government has reached agreement to offset this cost through tax credits but the majority remains unresolved. The Lot 1 Contractor is owed an additional US$490,000 for explosive import costs due to new government regulations. The procurement for preparing the concept design and bidding documents for ELWA Junction-Red Light intersection -Coca Cola Factory road section is in progress and the consultant is likely to be hired by October, 2016.

v The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT I. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL 1. At project appraisal, Liberia was one of Africa’s poorest countries with a gross domestic product (GDP) per capita of US$210 in 2009. The country managed to sustain its growth amidst these challenges with a GDP growth of 9.7 percent in 2007, 7.1 percent in 2008, and 4.9 percent (estimated) in 2009.2 Liberia’s economic growth slowed down in 2009 due to low commodity prices resulting from the global economic downturn. Infrastructural loses from the 14-year civil war presented serious challenges to economic development despite the post-war political stability in Liberia. Extensive destruction of basic infrastructure, absence of maintenance, poor education and health indicators, limited transportation and communications connectivity, ethnic loyalties, and weak public institutions limited the use of natural wealth and citizenry cohesion to promote sustainable and broad-based income growth.3 Most of the 10,000 km of existing roads were in extreme disrepair and non-motorable during the rainy seasons and were, therefore, identified as a priority need for development and infrastructural rehabilitation during the development of the Poverty Reduction Strategy (PRS). 2.

In 2008, through the National Transport Policy and Strategy initiated by the World Bank and supported by the German Technical Cooperation (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit, GTZ), medium- and long-term goals were set to revamp the road sector. The goals focused on contracting arrangement, maintenance strategy, and institutional formulation. A self-standing Infrastructure Implementation Unit (IIU) with greater decision-making authority was established out of this strategy in 2009. The IIU was a transformation of the Special Implementation Unit which was set up in 2006 under the Ministry of Public Works (MPW) to be the implementation unit for IDA and other donor-funded infrastructure projects with the broader aim of improving capacity in the road sector. 3. To direct Liberia’s reformation agenda, a Country Assistance Strategy (CAS) was also prepared in 2009 through joint funding from IDA, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and the African Development Bank (AfDB). The CAS was designed to respond to core strategic areas mostly affected by the civil war, which included intervention on peace and security, economic revitalization, strengthening of governance and rule of law, and infrastructure and basic services provided in the PRS in 2008. The CAS had three strategic themes: (a) rebuilding core state functions and institutions; (b) rehabilitating infrastructure to jump-start economic growth; and (c) facilitating pro-poor growth.

Infrastructure rehabilitation and long-term management and preservation of assets were identified as major prerequisites for attainment of the long-term CAS outcomes of improving services, economy, and social conditions. 4. The Liberia Road Asset Management Project (LIBRAMP) became a key part of the CAS due to road maintenance and funding needs of the government. The project’s aim was not to only reconstruct damaged roads but also to enhance connectivity between urban and rural areas as well as between Liberia and its neighboring countries to expand trade and provide access to services and jobs to catalyze Liberia’s growth and sustainable development in the road sector. For this purpose, the Monrovia-Guinea border road corridor was chosen for the project. The corridor is important and was core to the nation’s reconstruction as it connects the five largest cities in Liberia and provides cross-border connections. For the long-term preservation of the road asset, the project preparation recognized the need for adequate financing for routine maintenance (RM) and periodic maintenance (PM) through annual budgets and anticipated donor support for maintenance as well. The project preparation also envisaged further improvement in the road network condition and was hence designed to discuss a more reliable and bigger funding for road maintenance through the establishment of a road fund.

The project was hence endorsed with funding support from international donors which was coordinated by the 2Project Appraisal Document (2011) 3World Bank, 2018. Systematic Country Diagnostic. https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/1d454fc8-d4d3-5904-8cca- 813118460961/content Page 1 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT World Bank. LIBRAMP was in a position to receive financing from the World Bank as well since Liberia had become IDA creditworthy post recovery and progress in implementing the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) reform in June 2010 including the Public Financial Management Law. 5. LIBRAMP design benefited from lessons from existing projects, mostly those on output-based contracts. The output-based contract was the first in Liberia and the sub-region. A long term (ten-year) output and performance-based road contract (OPRC) approach which required commitment from all parties was opted for the design of LIBRAMP to provide both rehabilitation and maintenance on the Monrovia-Guinea border road corridor. The long-term OPRC was to provide the road network in Liberia with a consistent and appropriate level of service over the medium term instead of using a series of traditional contracts. The method aimed to ensure institutional development over the long term while safeguarding the road lifespan with an efficient maintenance mechanism. Project Development Objectives (PDOs) 6.

The PDO as defined in the PAD and financing agreement was to “support the Recipient’s efforts to reduce transport costs along the road corridor from Monrovia to the Guinea border and to maintain the road in good condition over a ten-year period” and remained unchanged until project completion. Figure 1 shows the project corridor which forms part of the core road network. Figure 1. Road Layout (Source: IIU) Key Expected Outcomes and Outcome Indicators 7. Two PDO outcomes were targeted: (a) to reduce transport costs along the road corridor from Monrovia to the Guinea border and (b) to maintain the road in good condition over a ten-year period. Four PDO indicators were assigned to measure the two outcomes in the results framework (RF). The PDO indicators are as follows: Page 2 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT Outcome 1 indicators: (i) Transport cost borne by road users including vehicle operating costs and monetary value of travel time (measured in terms of roughness reduction, International Roughness Index [IRI] rate in m/km), and (ii) direct project beneficiaries (number), of which female (percentage). Outcome 2 indicators: (i) Roads in good and fair condition as a share of total classified roads (percentage) and (ii) share of rural population with access to an all-season road (percentage) Components 8.

The project design included two essential components at an initial cost of US$249.4 million, of which US$108.9 million was under the Liberia Reconstruction Trust Fund (LRTF), US$67.7 million by IDA, and US$72.8 million by the Government of Liberia (GOL). The project underwent four restructurings (with two additional financings) that led to the addition of two new components during implementation. RELEVANCE OF PDO Assessment of Relevance of PDOs and Rating 15. The project activities were well-aligned with Liberia’s National Development Plans (NDPs). Specifically, the project was aligned with the Pro-Poor Agenda for Prosperity and Development (PAPD) for 2018 to 2023 which is the second in the series of the five-year NDPs.5 The PAPD outlined a development outcome that sought to increase economic activity and connectivity through critical roads under its Pillar 2—economy and jobs. The specific road corridor connects the urban areas within Nimda County to the rural areas and the neighboring country, Guinea, and provides access to jobs and services among counties and between the rural and urban areas.

The Monrovia-Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea border road corridor is the country’s backbone and connects places along the corridor to the capital, Monrovia, as well as to Guinea and Sierra Leone. The road is part of the Core Roads for Economic Growth and Transformation (CREAT)6 created to connect areas with high developmental potential with the far-flung less developed areas. The road corridor has a high potential to bring socioeconomic development to Liberia. 16. The PDO remained consistent with the current World Bank Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for Liberia for the period FY19 to FY24.7 The PDO is specifically aligned to Pillar 3 of the CPF which looks at “narrowing the infrastructure gap to foster more equitable development nationwide” and more particularly addresses Objective 7 which aims at 5 https://globalnaps.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/liberia-national-development-agenda-pro-poor-agenda.pdf 6 The total length of CREAT is 3,322 km and includes already implemented paved roads (700.46 km) to be maintained under potential long-term OPRC or PBMC methods. 7 https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/374031541438293964/pdf/liberia-cpf-11012018-636768792698663889.pdf Page 5 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT “improved access to utilities, markets, and community services.” The PDO’s relevance is further emphasized in the priority policy areas and development interventions in the Systematic Country Diagnostic (SCD) for FY20.

PDO 1: Reduce transport costs along the road corridor from Monrovia 19. Achievement of PDO 1 is rated Substantial since it was achieved and the road remains in a good condition to benefit users in term of reduction in transport-related cost. 20. The project achieved its target outcomes. Prior to the project interventions, the surface of the road corridor was in very poor condition with a mix of surface types including asphalt concrete from Monrovia to Gbarnga, a deteriorated asphalt surface treatment from Gbarnga to Ganta, and a gravel surfaced road between Ganta and the Guinea border (2 km).

The project financed the rehabilitation, including sections of new construction and annual RM of the corridor through the OPRC, which improved the road surface and riding condition for both urban and rural sections. The road’s IRI, which measures the ride quality, improved from 12 percent to less than 3 percent after the rehabilitation. The last IRI was measured in November 2024, after the project had closed, and recorded an average IRI of 2.19 percent, lesser than the 3 percent target set for June 2024. An actual vehicle operation cost (VOC) and delay reduction measurement would have been more useful. Notwithstanding, the IRI is considered a proxy indicator for VOC and delay levels, therefore, the low IRI recorded four months after project close is indicative of better riding quality which potentially will result in reduced VOC, travel delays, and transport costs. A road user survey was also undertaken to determine user satisfaction regarding the improved road before project closing. Out of the 1,000 respondents, 62 percent indicated that their travel time has reduced and were satisfied with the road improvement. 21. The improved road and intersection in Monrovia directly benefited 362,905 people in the rural areas as anticipated and people in the urban area in Monrovia. The benefits were in various forms from reduction in travel time and increased access to jobs and services as noted from the survey, and potentially a reduction in VOC, among other expected benefits.

Almost two thirds (63 percent) of the survey participants indicated that the road has made it convenient for them to access their homes and basic amenities like school, work, market, and hospital. With the improvement in connectivity and accessibility, a boost in the national economy is expected through increased intercity trade among the corridor cities8, counties, and regional trade and commerce with neighboring countries like Guinea. 8 This road connects four of the country’s five largest cities: Monrovia, Ganta, Buchanan, Kakata, and Gbarnga. The project was designed to efficiently restore the destroyed road infrastructure and low institutional capacity in Liberia’s road sector after the war. With the deplorable road condition and economic challenges in Liberia, the traditional input-based road maintenance contract which required three different contracts for rehabilitation, RM, and PM works was deemed a more expensive, less efficient, and less attractive option.

Adopting an OPRC with longer duration and a single entity for all three works presented a better choice for accountability and efficiency and a good avenue for long-term capacity building for the road sector. Per the countries condition at the time, the 10 years OPRC was a more attractive option for private sector participation in the form of CEs. 43. The project was structured on lessons learned from OPRC projects worldwide. Liberia is the first in the sub- region to undertake an OPRC and the project design benefited from the lessons learnt from ongoing or completed OPRCs in some countries.14 The lessons highlighted potential risk, payment model for both rehabilitation and maintenance works, long term network management interventions to spread the contractor’s risk, and World Bank inclusion throughout the project life. The project leveraged the World Bank’s convening power and technical expertise on OPRCs and in coordinating development partners through LTDF administration. B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION 44. The project was expected to be implemented in ten years to include three years of rehabilitation and seven years of maintenance but took 13 years. At project close, the RM had not been fully implemented and the revised PM had not been started. The challenges and successes during implementation were attributable to the factors discussed below. a. Factors subject to government control 45.

Key among the implementation challenges was the inability of the GOL to provide its overall funding contribution of US$47.8 million. Liberia faced numerous macroeconomic constraints which led to an International Monetary Fund (IMF) program in 2019 and the GOL’s failure to contribute to finance claims and RM and PM activities under Component 1 as well as RAP implementation.15 The RM was suspended on October 1, 2022, and the asphalt overlay activity under the PM was never started. The GOL’s failure to finance RAP implementation delayed site handover to the CE and rehabilitation works by close to 17 months. Sites were fully handed over to the CE at the end of July 2015, after work commencement in 2012 and 2013 for Lot 1 and 2, respectively. While US$10 million IDA funds under the Urban and Rural Infrastructure Rehabilitation Project (URIRP) financed RAP compensation payments for Lot 1 and Lot 2, US$5 million under LIBRAMP AF2 was sourced for the urban road section. 14 Countries in Latin America (Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay), South Asia (India), and Africa (Chad, Zambia, and Botswana) were identified with OPRC experience at appraisal. 15 RAP compensation for Lots 1 and 2 was provided from IDA resources under the URIRP (P113099) while for the 6.1 km urban road it was from IDA resources under AF2 of LIBRAMP.
