Aside from the RAP implementation, the country’s regulations changes and contractual noncompliance issues also delayed the project. New regulation from the Ministry of Lands, Mines, and Energy to restrict importation of explosives to a single entity with limited capacity disrupted the activities of the CEs, leading to delays and uncertainty regarding quarrying activities. The reversal of the tax exemption agreement on fuel imports by the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) contributed to the cost overrun from claims and the delay in payment thereof also resulted in accrued interests on the tax levies collected from the CE. 47. Contract administration lapses and delay in decision-making by the IIU led to claims with associated interests. Late and lack of reporting on pertinent issue like the theft of five cancelled cheques16 for RAP compensation and other noncompliance issues by the IIU was observed. The government through the project’s private bank, Liberian Bank for Development and Investment (LBDI), has recouped, as of 2017, all the stolen cheques which were categorized as ineligible expenses. The procurement team of the IIU on the other hand showed in-depth experience in handling IDA and other donor-funded projects and their familiarity with World Bank guidelines and procedures was found useful for project delivery. 48. Low oversight and compliance enforcement by the GOL and the IIU on environmental and social (E&S) issues slowed project progress and performance.

Incidences of E&S noncompliance led to suspension, downgrading of implementation performance, and additional cost implications. The largest was the forceful eviction of the 3,227 registered and unregistered petty traders by the GOL on July 12, 2021, to give RoW to the CE at the Redlight intersection of the 6.1 km urban road section. The lack of compliance of the CE with the Environmental Management Plan (EMP) and Health, Safety, and Environmental Management Plan (HSEMP) implementation particularly on restoration of quarry sites was also a key environmental issue. For noncompliance with the EMP and contractor’s HSEMP, there were no explicit penalties imposed on the CE, leaving the MC with limited means to manage non-conformance. The investigation and preparation of a remedial action plan for the OP4.12 noncompliance regarding the petty traders led to about 18 months of delay to the project. The action plan included compensation for the petty traders for income loss and property damage to the petty traders over the 180-day eviction period. 49. In view of the GOL’s inability to fund the petty traders’ compensation, IDA financing of US$2.15 million under the Rural Economic Transformation Project (RETRAP) AF2 17 has been arranged.

Beside the challenge of the IIU and Grievance Redress Committee (GRC) in locating the unregistered transient traders, the implementation of the compensation could not be completed at the project closing due to a RETRAP Legal Agreement covenant.18 All E&S issues which could not be completed during the project tenure are captured in the action plan in table 7.1 in annex 7. b. Factors outside the control of the government, IIU, and World Bank 50. The project experienced two major disease outbreaks during its implementation: the Ebola virus in 2014 and the SARS COV-2 (COVID-19) in 2020. Even though the EVD outbreak was covered under force majeure contractually, the death of four project staff in the Lot 2 campsite led to the site closing and halting of activities from August 2014 for about seven months. The COVID-19 pandemic slowed down work on the 6.1 km urban section from March 2020, delaying the urban site handover till December 2020, and led to the termination of the contract of the Lot 1 MC which was taken over by the MC for Lot 2. 16 The PFMU cancelled 21 ‘returned’ cheques totaling US$118,796 out of which five worth US$16,748 were stolen. 17 The IDA funding of AF2 to the RETRAP(P181083) financed the entire petty traders’ compensation under a contingency arrangement approved by the Regional Vice President (RVP).

The compensation was part of the action plan to correct the OP4.12 noncompliance involving 1,653 semi-mobile petty traders and 1,574 fully transient petty traders who were forcefully evicted from the urban section from June 2021 to February 2022. 18 The compensation of US$180,000 for the registered petty traders is to be released under a contingency category after the RVP and restructuring. Page 13 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT c. Factors subject to the control of World bank and government 51. The long project duration resulted in some significant staff turnover among key players. Over the last 13 years, the project has seen four World Bank Task Team Leaders, two MC contracts for Lot 1, four sector ministers with varying interest in institutional reforms, and other sectoral staff changes. The procedural handing-overs and assimilation of new staff slowed down decision-making generally and disrupted progress on the institution reform especially in 2013. The long tenure also exposed the project to prolonged price fluctuation and foreign exchange losses. IV. BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME A. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) M&E Design 52. The PDO achievement and progress were designed to be measured by output and outcome indicators.

The indicators measured two thematic areas: (a) road network development and performance which measured the improvement in physical road network condition and benefit in transport cost to road users and (b) institutional development which measured the progress and results of capacity-building interventions under intermediate indicators. The project control team/IIU were assigned the responsibility of the daily project management and overall monitoring and reporting on the RF at appraisal while the MCs assisted the IIU by regular monitoring of compliance and service-level criteria of the road. M&E TA and training was provided under Component 2. 53. The RF was clearly defined. Baseline and target values as well as methodology, data source, and frequency of data collection were defined at appraisal and revised where necessary under the various restructurings. The methodologies for each indicator were succinct; however, for an indicator like the transport cost borne by road users, actual VOC and travel time measurements would have been more appropriate compared to the use of IRI which is a proxy. Also, the indicator to measure maintenance, ‘roads maintained’, was not succinct as it failed to differentiate PM from RM and did not account for a time-bound result as was the design. M&E Implementation 54. The RF was revised through three of the four restructurings.

At the close of the project, the RF consisted of four PDO indicators and twelve intermediate indicators from the appraisal’s four PDO and six intermediate indicators. The changes in indicators, outlined in table 2 were due to (a) removal or reduction of certain activities due to lack of counterpart financing, leading to the dropping of some indicators and (b) scale-up of component and activities to support road safety and enhance connectivity between urban and rural areas. Data collection for the PDO indicators was robustly done till June 2022, when data collection and monitoring was halted due to project suspension. The PDO indicators were not measured from 2022 till project close. 55. The IIU did not hire or designate an M&E specialist to oversee the RF data collection, review, and evaluation. While the IRI and Component 1 intermediate indicators were collected by the CE under the supervision of the MC, the other PDO and intermediate indicators were to be collected and reported by the IIU. Collection, collation, dissemination, and monitoring of the data from the various entities was poorly done resulting in inconsistency in reporting on values and updating of indicators between the World Bank and the client.

Some indicators like ‘hired female staff in the IIU’ and ‘percentage of citizen complaints addressed within seven days’, which was to monitor the performance of the grievance Page 14 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT redress mechanism under the Argo app,19 were never reported, even though data was measured. Others like IRI were not keenly monitored and measured as designed. The mid-term review report by the MC recommended a person within the IIU to be designated as the M&E lead officer, which was not addressed. 56. The economic and social indicator recommended during appraisal to support future investment decision- making was not undertaken. The indicator was to measure travel pattern information, agriculture prices, transport cost as a share of household income, access to health and education facilities, and other accessibility and mobility related information. These indicators which were not part of the RF was intended for future planning and a broad assessment of the investment impact. A road user satisfaction survey was undertaken in place of the social and economic studies. The survey was however carried out eight years after rehabilitation was completed and may record under- or over-estimated views of respondents due to the long recall period. M&E Utilization 57. The PDO and intermediate indicators were useful in monitoring project progress and ensuring compliance to quality.

The progress on indicators was instrumental in the overall decision-making of key players for additional financing, extension of the closing date, and payment to the CE. The capacity-building indicator under Component 2 is expected to improve the preparedness of the IIU toward their reformation into a road authority. Justification of Overall Rating of Quality of M&E 58. The overall quality of the project’s M&E is assessed as Modest. The project’s M&E framework was well-designed; however, it would have benefitted more from inclusion of the social/economic indicators and actual measurements of VOCs to inform other future investments’ decision-making. Recruitment of an M&E specialist was also required to monitor and provide recommendable actions to better address the lapses in the framework. B. ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND FIDUCIARY COMPLIANCE 59. The overall E&S performance of the project, as of June 30, 2024, is rated Unsatisfactory while the risk remained Substantial. The project triggered three safeguard policies: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11), and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). LIBRAMP was categorized as a Category “B” E&S risk project. Ensuring adequate compliance with E&S safeguards in both the urban and rural sections of LIBRAMP has been persistently challenging. Several factors have significantly contributed to the project's low E&S performance, including: • Client’s technical and operational capacities.

The client has faced difficulties in meeting the technical and operational requirements necessary for E&S compliance. • Contractors’ and subcontractors’ noncompliance. There has been a notable failure among contractors and subcontractors to adhere to their contractual obligations. • Funding issues. There has been a lack of or delayed funding to implement various resettlement plans. • Inadequate regulatory monitoring. Insufficient regulatory oversight has further exacerbated the compliance issues. 60. During the implementation phase, the project's safeguards performance was downgraded due to unresolved noncompliance issues. These include nonpayment of income loss compensation to the forcefully evicted petty traders, 19Argo is a smartphone-based app and online tool which was implemented by the IIU for enhancing project monitoring, transparency, and social accountability. The app will provide a georeferenced dashboard of incidents/reports by users who provide feedback using smartphones or text messages. Page 15 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT unresolved quarry site issues for the five quarry sites, and delayed reporting and resolution of fatal accidents. Overall, the project has not fully complied with the policy requirements and objectives of OP 4.01 and OP 4.12.

To address the outstanding remedial actions, table 7.1 in annex 7 presents a post-closing plan aimed at addressing the outstanding remedial actions during the one-year defect liability period. Also, contingency funding of US$2.2 million under the RETRAP AF2 is provided to ensure compensation payments for income losses and property damages to the forcefully evicted petty traders. The World Bank will continue to provide hands-on post-closure implementation supervision until all plans outlined in annex 7 are implemented. Fiduciary 61. The project fiduciary risk was Substantial during appraisal and remained same till project closure. Financial Management 62. The PFMU at the Ministry of Finance was assigned the financial management (FM) responsibility at appraisal since the management arrangements at the MPW did not conform with the World Bank's minimum FM requirements. With PFMU’s good structure, internal controls, and experience in managing donor funds, the residual FM risk was rated Moderate at appraisal. The FM performance commenced Satisfactorily; however, mainly due to the GOL's failure to fulfill its counterpart contribution of US$48.7 million which formed 18 percent of the project cost, the ratings dropped to Moderately Satisfactory at project closing with a high risk rating. Overall disbursement at the project closing stood at 100 percent for both IDA funds and LRTF contribution.

In terms of legal covenants, the project submitted the interim financial reports and the audited reports on time with few delays; the delays were not more than 30 days. Procurement 63. The IIU was responsible for the procurement and hired two procurement specialists as stipulated in the legal covenants. The project procurement risk and performance were Substantial and Moderately Satisfactory, respectively, at closure. The procurement implementation status recorded positive progress. A total of 30 contracts planned were awarded and completed. In the procurement process, the project used appropriate market approaches and considerations were given to size, value, and complexity of the procurement package, and all were consistent with the legal framework. Clear procurement documents, proportionate to the need, were used to encourage broad participation from potential competitors. IDA procurement procedures have been well followed, both through open market and national markets methods. The Agency effectively managed contracts to ensure delivery per the contract conditions. The selection and award processes were carried out effectively, efficiently, and transparently. Contracts and payment documents were uploaded in the Systematic Tracking of Exchanges in Procurement (STEP) system promptly, except for a few activities that the project finally uploaded during closure. No visible risks were observed except for the delay in uploading the contract and payment for a few activities.

Also, it was observed that many activities were cancelled after they were planned. Post- procurement review was conducted, and no serious procurement issues or gaps were found. It was obvious that the project kept its procurement specialists throughout the project life, and this continuity helped the procurement implementation. C. BANK PERFORMANCE Quality at Entry 64. The project design was anchored on the World Bank’s experience and relationship with the GOL since 2005. The World Bank team provided advice on the choice of the contract type, risk allocation measures, and institutional strengthening based on a lot of factors, including lessons learned on OPRC, prevailing post-war condition of infrastructure, low capacity of government and institutions to maintain road infrastructure, and lack of attractiveness of Liberia’s business Page 16 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT environment to the private sector at the time. The project design galvanized resources from donors under the LRTF and from IDA credit to provide lasting infrastructure at less risk to government and more attractive conditions for private sector participation as CEs or MCs. 65. The project design should have been scoped to available funds. The macroeconomic condition in Liberia did not support its ability to co-finance the project in 2011, during the project appraisal.

Even though some economic stability was observed resulting in the completion of the HIPC program in 2010, as at 2009 and during the project preparation, the global financial crisis had affected Liberia’s economy resulting in GDP values dropping from a growth of 7.1 percent in 2008 to 4.9 percent (estimated) in 2009. The GOL’s ability to co-finance was not likely especially since at the time, IDA financing was being sourced for RAP implementation for the URIRP.20 These prevailing conditions should have informed the design of the project to be based on available funds to avoid cancellation of the road maintenance activities. Quality of Supervision 66. The World Bank team successfully provided adequate guidance on contract management and performance monitoring to the IIU staff and the sector. Task teams provided intensive handholding support to augment the institutional arrangement. Twenty-four intensive missions were undertaken, which included the right skill mix to provide the necessary guidance to IIU staff and its management. In addition, the World Bank team provided enhanced interactions including video conferences and monthly review meetings with the IIU. Beside these, technical missions by specialized teams were undertaken to provide guidance on pertinent issues on E&S and gender-based violence/sexual exploitation and abuse.

The World Bank proactively supported the government in the one-year extension of the LRTF closing date to avoid losing US$4.84 million, secured US$90 million AF under IDA credit, and supported the restructuring of the project to achieve the project objectives. 67. Some decisions during implementation bore inherent risks. Even though the team supported the project management effectively, in the absence of counterpart funding, the decision to rehabilitate the 6.1 km urban road because of challenges with human congestion at the Redlight Junction and ELWA intersection under Subcomponents 1.2 and 1.3 was debatable given the extent of social issues involving petty traders in a context where the project was not supposed to finance RAP. The urban section also had no maintenance component which was not consistent with the project’s OPRC direction. Dropping the urban road subcomponents was among the three options of the World Bank to the GOL during the mid-term review to inform subsequent restructuring. The funds used for the intersection and urban section could have financed the entire PM and some RM. The 20-year road life would potentially have been safeguarded and the non- compliances issues related to the petty traders which is still not fully resolved to date would have potentially been avoided. 68.

The team was proactive in ensuring continual engagement on road asset management and institutional strengthening through the design of SECRAMP.21 Under Component 2 of SECRAMP, the MPW and Ministry of Transport will continue the implementation of the road safety action plan designed under LIBRAMP. Also, under Component 3, TA and capacity-building support for transformation of the IIU into a full-fledged road agency is being continued. This arrangement was in anticipation of the government’s inability to undertake the IIU reformation into a road authority capable of taking strategic decisions on road maintenance before the LIBRAMP closing date. Justification of Overall Rating of Bank Performance 69. Based on the above, the overall World Bank Performance is rated Moderately Satisfactory. 20 URIRP, which was effective in 2009 and closed in 2017, was financed by IDA and LRTF financing and US$8.0 million of IDA funds. AF2 under URIRP made provision for RAP compensation for both URIRP and LIBRAMP. 21 SECRAMP was approved in 2018 and will close in 2027. One part of its PDO is to improve institutional capacity to manage the road sector. Page 17 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT D. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 70. The risk to sustainability of the development objective is high. 71. The road asset is at risk of potential deterioration due to lack of maintenance.

The project closed with incomplete maintenance works due to lack of counterpart funding. Liberia’s road asset is valued at 73 percent of GDP22 indicating that the investment required for rehabilitation, upgrade, and maintenance exceeds governments resources. The government financing for maintenance is not reliable especially as commitments made to the CEs at annex 7 have not been paid to date. This puts the Monrovia-Guinea border road at risk of losing its current good condition rating. Early deterioration and reduced safety along the road are expected in the absence of RM and PM. 72. Lack of axle weighing stations along the road corridor exposes the road to early defects and deterioration. In view of the project duration, the project recommended the installation of an axle weighing station by the CE to check overloading to substantiate compensation claims on account of deteriorations due to overloading. This was not built either by the government as a road preservation measure or the CE. The absence of weighing stations along the road corridor exposes the road to uncontrolled overloading and early deterioration of sections as observed from the pavement assessment report. Already 33 km and 17 km are observed to have some defects and are recommended to be corrected and overlain with asphalt. 73. Further institutional reform is necessary to ensure sustainability of the road asset.

The creation of the road maintenance fund, transformation of the IIU into a road authority, and streamlining of the MPW as a policy and maintenance planning entity are all enshrined in the reformation. Whilst the road maintenance fund was created, reforms at the IIU and MPW are pending and necessary to provide a more organized and regulated sector to concretize the trust and support of donor and bilateral groups. Investment through capacity building and TAs have already been made in the road sector to undertake efficient asset management and strategic investments. The autonomy of the IIU as an authority will enhance its ability to make decisions and potentially limit the government’s interference. It is hoped that the continuation of the reformation process under SECRAMP will see the finalization of the institutional reform. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 74. The OPRC was a useful road contract approach to provide continuous preservation of the road asset and institutions in Liberia over 10 years. For a similar country context of having experienced long civil wars and major road infrastructure and institutional capacity losses, the use of a long-term OPRC of ten years provided benefits in institutional capacity development on contract and project management as well as on road asset management practices.

The ten-year OPRC provided the space for uninterrupted maintenance of the road asset after rehabilitation as compared to the traditional method and can be fully implemented to all RM and PM provided there are (a) dedicated funds for all activities, (b) well-structured contracts to ensure conformance by all parties, (c) training of contractors on OPRC, and (d) adequate and well-designed projects. 75. Where ten-year models are not feasible, a shorter duration OPRC could be equally beneficial as an asset management contract tool in countries like Liberia. The ten-year OPRC has the potential to expose contracts to risk related to institutional inadequacies, price fluctuations, and contingencies. In view of this, a shorter duration for OPRC planned for rehabilitation and RM could be suitable. In this way, PM can feasibly be part of the project design 22The road asset value (RSV) was based on the available data on replacement/reconstruction value of the road network as recorded in the RSDP Report, 2023 Page 18 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT recommendations rather than an actual output of the project to avoid or reduce the extent of damages allocated to clients and the government when they are not realized due to inadequate funds as observed in VOs 4 and 1 in annex 7. 76. The payment model for the OPRC was suitable for the long-term project and Liberia’s context in keeping the CEs at post.

Some parts of the rehabilitation lump sum payments were extended into the maintenance payments . The challenges related to force majeure and nonpayment of maintenance work could potentially have disincentivized the CEs from undertaking the maintenance works for six years. Rehabilitation payments were completed per the model in 2022 for both Lots 1 and 2 at which year the CEs suspended the RM. The payment model however was not supported by HDM- 4 for economic analysis. As the OPRC remains useful, revision in HDM-4 should factor the various models to make economic analysis easier. 77. In view of the lack of counterpart financing, which was a major drawback on implementation in Liberia, future operations should ensure that counterpart funds are available before their inclusion in the financing matrix. The situation also exposes the need for government to expand the revenue base for the NRF for maintenance to include other sources like tolling and axle load control which are absent in Liberia. Axle load control besides providing revenue, reduces road deterioration from overloading. The adoption of the RSDP, both for institutional strengthening and streamlining of government investment by allocating available road sector funding according to evidence-based planning is hence crucial. The plan encourages the scoping of projects based on available funds and exploration of other funding options from the private sector to support government budgets on maintenance.

The plan also highlights the significant role of donors in addressing development issues and LIBRAMP provides a good example of this role. The project’s achievements shows that meaningful results can be achieved at scale when partners combine resources to collectively address development challenges. LIBRAMP was realized through funding from IDA and multiple donors under the LRTF. 78. For better data collection and collation and assessment of projects, especially those that are performance- oriented and have longer tenure like the OPRC, the nomination or hiring of an M&E specialist is necessary and their enforcement in the legal covenant is recommended. The specialist would support the update, review, and provide recommendations for adjustment to indicators over the long term. The M&E specialist will also support the monitoring of project performance to enhance delivery of projects. 79. The forceful eviction of the petty traders by the Liberian government highlights a lack of widespread awareness of Bank Policy and Procedures on social and environmental issues, particularly among government officials and establishments. It is therefore important for projects to encourage regular and continuous education and engagements with stakeholders, especially decision-making officials and leaders in government to ensure that both new and existing officials remain informed and up-to-date with current Bank procedures.

EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS I. Introduction 1. This annex documents the economic evaluation of LIBRAMP. The analysis used the CBA approach and quantified the construction costs, RM, and PM of the rehabilitation of the 249 km corridor, and the benefit analysis of lower VOC, passenger time savings, and lower accidents.

These were based on (a) traffic volume, (b) estimated travel cost, (c) investment and maintenance cost, and (d) IRI values. The annex also briefly summarizes the non-quantified economic and social benefits including sustainable job creation resulting from the ten-year OPRC; efficiency gains and administrative cost savings for the government (IIU); and a potential to foster restructuring and performance improvement within the road sector. However, due to the complexity of attribution and limitation of the information, these benefits were not quantified. 2. At ex ante analysis was conducted using the HDM-4 model for Lot 1 and the RED model for Lot 2, assuming a design life of 20 years, with 2010 as the base year. The appraisal of Lot 1 urban section - Coca Cola to ELWA junction was done in 2017 following the scale up and did not include maintenance. The project was expected to generate an NPV of US$48.8 million and an EIRR of 23 percent for Lot 1 rural (Monrovia Red Light-Gbarnga), an EIRR of 17.3 percent and NPV of $5.97 million for Lot 1 urban (Coca Cola to ELWA junction), and an NPV of US$9.2 million and EIRR of 18 percent for Lot 2 (Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea border). 3. The ex post economic evaluation utilized the HDM-4 model for both lots, as RED is deemed inappropriate for the evaluation of the paved road.

According to the Africa Transport Technical Note (1999), road deterioration equations, such as those in the HDM models, which account for road roughness over time, based on condition, traffic, and maintenance characteristics, are not implemented in RED. Instead, RED uses the concept of average service levels, which is suitable for low-volume unpaved roads. RED assumes a constant average level of service for both with- and without-project cases over the 20-year analysis period, which is considered inappropriate. The ICR analysis therefore used vehicle characteristics, utilization data, travel time costs, and climate information derived from the previous RED analysis but adjusted as necessary in HDM-4. 4. Both the appraisal and ex post analysis included construction costs, RM, and PM. The PM cost and cost of RM from 2022 are assumed and not actual costs during the project implementation tenure. Construction and RM cost up to 2022 were based on actual construction and RM expenses. Calibration was performed at Level 1 with default values, as was done during the appraisal phase. Vehicle fleet data, traffic projections, and road pavement data were sourced from the initial appraisal documents and pavement evaluation reports completed at the end of construction. II. Economic Analysis for Lot 1 Rural Section (Coca Cola to Gbarnga) and Urban Section (Coca Cola to ELWA junction) 5.

The planning horizon for the project ex post analysis was set at 20 years, with 2012 as the base year for the rural section and 2019 for the urban section. 6. Rural section. The project case scenario considered the actual costs incurred to date, amounting to US$156.92 million for construction and RM and estimated cost for PM and post-closure RM. This scenario resulted in an EIRR of 21.9 percent and an NPV of US$73.87 million, indicating a favorable economic outcome. 7. Urban section. This section did not align with the OPRC contract methodology as it included only construction of the urban road and ELWA roundabout whose cost totaled US$20.05 million, yielding an EIRR of 14.9 percent and an NPV of US$3.19 million, demonstrating economic viability, although lower than anticipated at appraisal. Page 30 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT III. Economic Analysis for Lot 2 - Gbarnga to Guinea Border Section 8. The analysis considered the actual costs paid up to March 2024, totaling $56.21 million for construction, RM, contingencies, emergency works as well as estimated cost for RM and PM during the 20-year project life. This scenario demonstrated economic viability, with an EIRR of 19.1 percent and an NPV of US$20.33 million. Additionally, the roadway length increased slightly and the cost per kilometer increased significantly compared to appraisal.

Although there are outstanding claims, the EIRR remained close, but the NPV was lower than anticipated. IV. Comparison of Project and Appraisal Economic Analysis 9. Several factors may account for the drop in the project appraisal NPV and EIRR at completion. These include variations in project road lengths at appraisal versus completion, differences in the projected cost per kilometer at appraisal, and the potential overestimation of benefits during appraisal. (a) Methodology. Appraisal analysis used the RED model for the Lot 2 economic assessment due to the deteriorated road condition (IRI = 12 m/km) at the time, with largely gravel or unpaved surfaces. In addition, there was insufficient data for the detailed analysis and deterioration modeling required by HDM-4. Therefore, the RED model was used. The ICR analysis, however, uses the more appropriate HDM-4 model for both lots. (b) Base year. The appraisal evaluation used a 20-year period starting in 2010, based on 2009 traffic data and VOC. However, the actual contract commenced in 2012 for Lot 1 rural and 2013 for Lot 2, considering the tender and procurement processes. Therefore, the ICR evaluation utilized a 2012 base year for Lot 1 rural, with 2012 VOC and utilization data and actual 2010 traffic data, and a 2013 base year for Lot 2, using 2013 VOC and 2012 traffic data. This provided the most up-to-date CBA. (c) Rehabilitation cost and payments.

For Lot 1 rural, the rehabilitation cost estimated during appraisal was US$96.4 million, while the actual project cost amounted to US$156.92 million, nearly double the estimated cost. On a per-kilometer basis, the costs were US$534,486 pre-construction and US$888,209 post- construction. Although appraisal estimated a construction period of three years, the actual construction took five years. However, payments were distributed over ten years as per the OPRC project design. For Lot 2, the appraisal estimated the rehabilitation cost at US$479,522 per kilometer, while the actual cost was also nearly double at US$801,397 per kilometer with a two-year construction period. However, the actual construction took three years, with payments spread over ten years according to the OPRC project design. (d) RM cost. This was estimated at US$6.8 million per year, compared to the actual cost of US$344,00 per year for Lot 1 rural, and US$2.1 million per year, compared to the actual cost of US$136,000 per year for Lot 2. The estimated cost was over ten times higher than the actual cost in the OPRC. At project closure, the constructed road was yet to receive its first 33 km of overlay, with an average IRI of less than 3 m/km, whereas the appraisal analysis planned for overlays in years eight and sixteen of the 20-year analysis period. (e) Traffic Volume (ADT). In 2009, Lot 1 rural had an ADT of 2,451 vehicles.

The projected growth rates were 35 percent from 2019–2012, 10 percent from 2012–2013, and 5 percent per year thereafter, leading to a cumulative ADT of 195,514 vehicles. However, the ex post cumulative traffic was assessed at 93,579 vehicles, indicating significantly lower demand anticipated. For Lot 2, ADT in 2009 was 1,473 vehicles with estimated growth rates of 35 percent from 2009–2012 and 10 percent from 2012–2013 resulting in an ADT of 4,385 vehicles, marking a 300 percent increase over five years. In contrast, the ex-post traffic volumes increased from an ADT of 1,540 vehicles to 2,520 vehicles over five years, marking a 164 percent increase from 2013– 2017. The cumulative ADT for the ex-post evaluation is assessed at 117,497 vehicles, compared to 71,587 Page 31 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT vehicles for the appraisal period, also significantly lower demand than anticipated. Despite the low traffic volume on both lots, overloading is suspected to be the cause of deterioration at some sections along the roadway. No recent traffic volume count data has been collected for the project road. 10. The project's viability at completion remains attractive, even though the cost per kilometer is higher for both lots. The economic analysis also indicates that the projected GHG emissions have been reduced from the projected 111,420 tons of CO2 per year at appraisal to 53,148.90 tons of CO2 per year. V. Conclusion 11.

In conclusion, the economic analysis for both Lot 1 and Lot 2 demonstrates economic viability under the project case scenarios, with EIRRs indicating higher returns than the planning discount rate of 12 percent. Overall, the project remains resilient to potential cost escalations, ensuring long-term sustainability and validating the investment in these infrastructure initiatives. Page 32 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT ANNEX 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS 1. The GOL has reviewed the findings of the World Bank’s ICR, and their comments have been addressed. The Borrower’s ICR has been submitted to the project team and is pending filing for information and referencing in WBDocs. The Borrower’s ICR is summarized below. 2. World Bank Performance. Throughout project implementation, seasoned World Bank professionals led task teams, bringing expertise in infrastructure, FM, procurement, and safeguards. Their diverse skills ensured tailored supervision and support, enabling necessary adjustments and restructurings to address challenges. Regular support from technical and fiduciary teams maximized the project's impact, with key decisions documented in Aide-Memoires. The World Bank's proactive oversight, timely 'no objections’, and expedited fund disbursements kept the project on track.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Despite challenges like high turnover of task team leaders affecting continuity, Monrovia-based World Bank staff provided continuous support, ensuring compliance and contributing significantly to the project's success. Overall, the implementation support and guidance provided by the World Bank were considered satisfactory, significantly contributing to the project's progress and success. 3. PDO achievement and key project impact factors. At project closing, all PDO outcome indicators met or exceeded targets, but intermediate results indicators had mixed results due to activity cancellations due to financial constraints and weak enforcement of zonal laws. The achievement of the project results was a result of (a) the OPRC contract approach which brought substantial efficiencies in contracting; it facilitated the completion of the Suakoko Highway rehabilitation and maintenance phase efficiently, (b) sectoral strengthening contributing to experience development and creating employment opportunities which presents broader socioeconomic benefits beyond infrastructure development, and (c) effective coordination among stakeholders, including government agencies, donors, and local communities, essential for aligning efforts and resources toward project objectives.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Collaboration between the MPW, local authorities, and community leaders facilitated smoother implementation and improved project outcomes, and the flexible management of the project allowed for adjustments to be made in response to changing circumstances. 4. Beside these key positive factors that contributed to the PDO achievement and project completion, issues such as (a) counterpart financing shortfall, (b) exchange rate fluctuations and cost escalation, (c) road safety and encroachment risks, (d) logistical transportation challenges resulting in difficulty in transporting construction materials and equipment to remote project sites posing logistical challenges, (e) nonpayment of government commitment, (f) funding delays from the GOL, (g) site handover delays, (h) impact of EVD and COVID-19 pandemics, (i) lack of coordination among utility agencies, waste management, and the MPW, and (j) challenges with petty traders and RoW and the subsequent noncompliance issues affected the project negatively. 5. Lessons learned. In summary, the LIBRAMP was hampered by financial, administrative, and coordination challenges. Nonpayment of government commitments, delays in fund releases, health crises, insufficient resources, and coordination issues all contributed to significant project delays and increased costs.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The project offered key lessons relevant to both the country and the region, including the following: • Government should ensure that future projects make provision for contingencies, including compensation for RAP and PAP funding commitments in loan agreements to prevent delays. • Local government involvement and enforcement of regulations are crucial for smooth project implementation. Page 33 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT • Detailed Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidelines for quarry mining and borrow pit exploitation are necessary for effective monitoring. • Investment in tools and procedures aligned with ECOWAS standards is essential for maintaining road quality. • Strengthening the Liberia National Road Fund and setting up a road agency is critical for effective road maintenance. • Prioritizing and operationalizing the road asset management system ensures efficient fund allocation. • Improved processes of fund flow from the LRA to the NRF will enhance predictable cashflow to that entity • New World Bank policies should be clearly defined and managed proactively to avoid delays and compliance issues. • Managing project commitments and ensuring timely payments can reduce excessive contractor claims and costs. • Measurable indicators for road safety activities other than training are necessary for effective implementation and monitoring.

CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL Context 1. At appraisal, Bihar was one of the faster growing low-income states in India, with 34 percent of its population living below the poverty line compared to a national average of 22 percent. About 90 percent of its population of 104 million was rural and about 76 percent of the population in north Bihar was subject to the recurring threat of floods. Bihar’s potential for growth in agriculture and agro‐based industries, tourism, handicrafts, and cottage industries was underutilized due to inadequate road infrastructure and market linkages. 2. About 60 percent of Bihar’s rural road network was unpaved and had several deficiencies, such as missing links, dilapidated bridges or absence of bridges, inadequate geometry, poor drainage, weak pavements, and missing road safety measures.

The network had also suffered severe damages due to floods, lack of maintenance, inadequate quality of initial construction, and overloading in some parts of the state. Inefficient sector management was also identified as a key challenge. “Road connectivity to each habitation”, with a goal of bringing all parts of the state within five hours of travel time from the state capital, Patna, was among Government of Bihar’s (GoB’s) top seven priorities in 2016. 3. As part of GoB’s priority of “Road connectivity to each habitation”, about 60,000 km of rural roads (50 percent of the total rural road network in the state) were constructed in the preceding decade leading to 2016, providing road access to 51 percent of its habitations. Several country and state level road development programs were in place to rehabilitate the remaining road network and provide access to all habitations in the state. The key programs were: (i) Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), the Government of India (GOI) funded program to provide all‐weather road access to all habitations with a population above 500; (ii) Mukhya Mantri Gram Sampark Yojana (MMGSY), the GoB funded program to provide road connectivity to habitations with population in the 250‐499 range, which were not covered under PMGSY; and (iii) Grameen Tola Sampark Nischaya Yojana (GTSNY), to connect habitations with a population below 250. The GoB’s rural roads program was organized around three key priorities: a.

Priority One: All‐weather-road access to the remaining 49 percent habitations through the PMGSY and MMGSY. The World Bank was engaged with PMGSY since its inception, through dialogue, technical assistance (TA), and a series of lending operations. b. Priority Two: Preserving existing road assets and upgrading them to acceptable standards. The road sector worked with a traditional focus on building and rehabilitating roads, which resulted in insufficient funds being directed for maintenance. Lack of planning and coordination with stakeholders in the sector which led to top-down fund allocation as opposed to allocations based on actual rehabilitation and maintenance needs to the road network, lack of an asset information database to support network-wide prioritization of rehabilitation and maintenance investments, and limited capacity within Rural Works Department (RWD) and contracting industry were other key issues that limited adequate asset management in the road sector. In this context, the RWD adopted Page 6 of 49 The World Bank Bihar Rural Roads Project (P155522) a maintenance policy, under which performance-based maintenance contracts were introduced on about 4,600 km of roads. The Bank supported RWD to prepare an Asset Management Plan (AMP) to introduce a new road asset management approach to deliver consumer-based priorities, such as a satisfactory level of riding quality and safety, at least cost over the long run. c.

Priority Three: Improved institutional effectiveness. Improve the pace and quality of delivery of RWD’s road programs by improving the quality of engineering designs and asset management, value for money, procurement performance, and by minimizing time and cost overruns. RWD required enhancement to its traditional way of doing business, to improve its performance and cope with the latest demands of both construction and maintenance. RWD’s business procedures were primarily suited for small works and had not kept pace with the demands, latest developments and innovations in the rural road sector. To this end, a Road Sector Modernization Plan (RSMP) was adopted by the RWD, which covered, inter alia, strengthening the Road Sector Policy Framework, streamlining and modernizing key business processes, climate resilient and cost‐effective engineering designs, and rural road safety. 4. Rationale for the project and for World Bank support. This Project proposed to support the MMGSY program by funding about eight percent of its planned road works and complementing it with knowledge support to enhance the management of rural roads in Bihar.

Bank support through the Project was expected to: (i) help enhance the quality of delivery of MMGSY by introducing cost‐effective designs, road safety engineering measures, improved quality of existing infrastructure, and better contract management practices to avoid time and cost‐over‐runs; and (ii) help gradually transform RWD into a modern and high performing road agency through knowledge support. The Bank was already engaged in the state’s road development program1, particularly through its long-standing engagement in PMGSY. The Project design was informed by the results and findings from these engagements and studies, for example, use of existing systems and procedure which were used under PMGSY, use of the PMGSY bid document, five-year mandatory maintenance inbuilt in construction contracts, and the use of the three-tier quality assurance mechanism. The Project provided an opportunity to make use of the analytical base and understanding of the sector derived from the Bank’s ongoing engagement in Bihar and enable the transfer of knowledge and coordination across different road programs in the state. 5. Alignment with Higher Level Objectives. The Project was aligned with the World Bank Group’s (WBG’s) goal of reducing poverty and promoting shared prosperity, and with WBG’s India Country Partnership Strategy (2013‐2017) priority of supporting low‐income states through three themes: integration, transformation, and inclusion.

The Project was expected to better integrate the rural population, businesses, and industries in Bihar’s remote and poorer districts with the national and state economy through better transport connectivity, as well as through improved integration with the strategic transport corridors passing through Bihar. It envisioned a transformational impact on rural poverty through the impact of improved road access on agricultural productivity, higher non‐farm employment opportunities, and increased rural wages. The Project was also in line with GoI’s development priorities at the time, which emphasized the development of rural roads to facilitate inclusive growth, economic development, and access to markets. ACHIEVEMENT OF PDOs (EFFICACY) Assessment of Achievement of Each Objective/Outcome 18. Approach to assessing the achievement of PDOs. The PDO comprises two elements: (i) improve rural road connectivity in Project districts; and (ii) enhance management of roads in Bihar. The first outcome is assessed through the impact of road improvements on the beneficiary communities and the second outcome by the Project’s impact in strengthening RWD’s capacity in managing roads in Bihar.

A split rating is applied in the evaluation of project efficacy due to following changes effected under Restructuring 2: (i) reduction of the PDO 1 outcome target for “Increased road connectivity to habitations”; (ii) dropping of the PDO 2 outcome target for “Improved asset management”; (iii) introduction of a new PDO 2 indicator “Pilot AI based system in districts within the state”; and (iv) the 80 percent reduction in financing allocated to Component 2. PDO 1: Improve rural road connectivity in project districts. 19. Key activities envisaged at appraisal were carried out during the Project, except for the reduction in the number of kms of roads improved and the dropping of activities under Sub-component 1.3. The key impacts of these activities are discussed below and the extent of achievement of the original and revised targets of PDO and intermediate level indicators relevant to PDO 1 is provided in Table 2. 20. Improved living standards through better road connectivity. The Project rehabilitated 2200kms of rural roads in Bihar, improving the connectivity of 1196 habitations and directly benefited about 838,240 people, 48 percent of which are women. Public consultations revealed that the roads now provide local farmers improved direct access to markets, which helps them to bypass intermediaries and thereby reduce costs.

The improved quality of the road pavements also ensures uninterrupted access to critical social services, such as health care and schools, which was earlier restricted during the rainy season as the roads became either muddy or were damaged. An assessment carried out4 to identify the impacts of the road improvements under the Project highlights that some communities have gained access to all-weather motorable roads for the first time, substantially improving their connectivity and accessibility. The improved roads have increased school attendance of students (of female students in particular) in some areas and have improved access to healthcare facilities due to the availability of different transport modes (e.g., ambulances, private vehicles). As most of the Bihar population lives in underdeveloped rural areas and one third of its population is poor, improvement in access to basic services and economic opportunities can contribute to economic development of these areas as well as reduce poverty in the long term. 21.

The case study cited earlier on the impact of the GoB’s broader MMGSY program, which the Project supported, further highlights the following benefits of improved road connectivity in the rural communities: reduced travel times to markets, schools and healthcare services; increased enrollment of students in schools (female students in particular); improved transportation of agricultural products with less wastage and shorter time using better transport modes as opposed to walking or using carts; and improved access to bigger agriculture markets. 22. Improved resilience of the road network through better maintenance. All project contracts included provisions for five-year routine maintenance to ensure uninterrupted connectivity. On completion of the five- year routine maintenance period, these roads will then be maintained under the GoB funded performance- based maintenance contracts as per GoB’s Rural Roads Maintenance Policy. This practice, which is supported by a state level policy, would help the long-term sustainability of the road network, as well as to reduce the fiscal impact of road rehabilitation costs to the state in the long run. However, a more systematic approach is required for the prioritization of roads for maintenance based on road condition and other technical criteria, as opposed to a blanket time-based maintenance policy. 23. The original scope of activities for the achievement of PDO 2 was modified during the second restructuring when development of the AMS was dropped, and piloting of the AI maintenance tool was introduced. The key impacts of these activities are discussed below and the extent of the achievement of PDO and intermediate indicators relevant to PDO 2 is provided in Table 3. 25. Introducing asset management practices in RWD. The Project contributed to introducing asset management practices to RWD and promoting its use in road maintenance. The AMP developed under the Project helped RWD identify the levels of service to be maintained for each road asset, the long-term financial plan for the rehabilitation and maintenance of roads, an asset valuation methodology for different road assets, human resource and capacity requirements for asset management, and requirements for an information system. The state funded the development of an AI tool to prioritize routine maintenance in the state’s road sector. The tool enables RWD to capture and digitally record (geo-tag) road conditions and take measures to rectify defects through contractors, using a digitalized process that links the relevant parties in one platform. The pilot inspected 1000 km of roads in Vaishali district and the RWD is planning to expand this system to the entire network. While the tool was expected to serve a similar purpose of an AMS, in practice, it does not provide the full benefits of a comprehensive AMS.

It only captures road condition data and does not consider other important criteria required for asset management such as traffic and crash data, connectivity, road structures etc., and does not support prioritizing capital and maintenance expenditure based on a systematic methodology considering such criteria. Furthermore, while the development of the AI tool was included as an activity under the Project with a corresponding PDO indicator, it was not financed by Project funds. Therefore, the tool cannot be attributed as a Project output. 26. Reduced cost of road rehabilitation with innovative pavement methods. The Project introduced two innovative road paving methods to reduce costs: (i) use of waste plastic in flexible pavements; and (ii) use of panel concrete in rigid pavements. These methods, which were used in more than 50 percent of the roads improved under the Project, saved around US$4.8 million (INR40.34 crores or approximately about 2 percent of the total cost) in road rehabilitation costs, and are now also being used in the MMGSY program. 27. Informed resilience management of the road network. A network level climate vulnerability assessment was carried out under the Project for 500 km of rural roads in 10 flood prone districts to identify the climate vulnerability of each road section based on the exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity of each road to the projected climate hazards for the period 2020-2039.

The study provides the RWD with: (i) a good basis to prioritize road improvements / maintenance based on climate vulnerability; and (ii) measures to improve the resilience and adaptation capacity of the road assets. The recommendations of the assessment are yet to be implemented but are being considered by RWD. 28. Informed improvements in integrated transport and logistics service provision. A diagnostic study was carried out to identify key transport and logistics challenges faced by selected micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Bihar and identify strategies to improve the transport and logistics network for their development. The study identified key barriers in (i) supply chains – such as lack of warehousing facilities, cold storage, poor quality roads, poor packaging; (ii) transport and logistics infrastructure – such as unpaved roads, low road densities in some districts; (iii) logistics services – such as fragmented trucking industry, gaps in skilled manpower, lack of automation; and (iv) policy and regulatory environment – such as lack of a state-wide policy on logistics. The recommendations to address challenges in road infrastructure management include (i) the development and improvement of transport infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and bypasses, and (ii) the Page 15 of 49 The World Bank Bihar Rural Roads Project (P155522) development of rural roads and first / last mile connectivity.

The RWD has submitted the report to the Industry Department for consideration of the recommendations to be implemented. 29. Informed road safety management. A Rural Road Safety Action Plan was developed identifying interventions required to improve road safety under the following pillars: (i) Road Safety Management – establishment of a rural road safety cell within RWD, setting up an rural road safety fund under Bihar Road Safety Council, capacity building and public consultations for safer road designs, (ii) Safer Roads – integrating road safety measures in the Detailed Project Report (DPRs), road safety audits at design stage, (iii) Safer Vehicles – safety features for different types of vehicles on rural roads, (iv) Safer Road Users – promoting community participation in identifying road safety issues, and increasing awareness, (v) Post-Crash Care – ensuring prompt emergency response, training for paramedics and first responders. The project also developed Road Safety Audit Checklists for different stages of road works in line with the Rural Road Safety Manual 2016 and the Manual on Road Safety Audit and provided training to DPR consultants on incorporating road safety measures in DPRs. These were complemented by the GoB’s road safety policy, which mandates road safety audits for all roads in the state that are longer than five kms. 30. Improved capacity and knowledge management.

415 RWD staff were trained on road management, including asset management, output and performance-based maintenance contracts (OPBMC), climate vulnerability assessments, cost-effective road designs, innovative pavement methods, bridge design, road safety, and the use of IT in road management. Project design had a clear rationale for the proposed activities. The majority of the activities under each component built on ongoing efforts and were presented with a clear justification. Rehabilitation of rural roads was a priority GoB program, and the roads were selected from the state core road network based on the habitations and linkages. Innovative and climate resilient technologies were proposed given the state’s vulnerability to floods as well as high material costs. Institutional strengthening activities were proposed to complement and / or take forward the identified activities under the RWD’s RSMP. 49. Readiness for implementation.

At approval, contracts for over 40 percent of the planned road length were in the process of being awarded and technical designs were being prepared for another 22 percent. The Page 20 of 49 The World Bank Bihar Rural Roads Project (P155522) draft asset management plan, human resources development strategy and the road safety action plan had been developed to initiate Component 2 activities. 50. Implementation arrangements were geared to the sustainability of project interventions. The Project was designed to use the existing government arrangements for implementing the MMGSY road program to ensure that enhancements introduced under the Project would be absorbed in the broader program of the state. B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION Factors generally subject to the control of government and/or implementing entities 51. Capacity constraints of the implementing agency, design consultants and contractors. The quality of work in the first batch of contracts was affected by the inadequate technical skills of the design consultants and RWD, as well as the weak contractor capacity. The DPRs developed for the first batch of contracts lacked proper culvert analysis and design, road safety measures (e.g., guardrail, traffic calming, and junctions), and effective cost saving measures. The technical audit carried out on the completed roads in this batch of contracts highlighted the lack of drains, poor riding quality, edge breaking, and pavement cracks.

RWD intends to implement the corrective measures recommended by the audit in the identified road sections. 52. Capacity gaps also affected the management of the Project’s environmental and social (E&S) safeguards. Until the MTR of the Project, the RWD did not have E&S specialists with the required skills and experience to ensure effective management of E&S issues and compliance with the Project’s safeguard’s instruments. Reporting on safeguards compliance and grievance redressal remained an issue during the first half of the Project, despite trainings provided by the Bank. In late 2020, the Project hired a firm to manage the Project’s E&S safeguards compliance and from mid-2021, safeguards management and compliance improved, and the Project began reporting more regularly on safeguards. 53. Shortage of staff assigned to manage the Project. The RWD staff and the Project Management Consultants (PMC) assigned to manage the Project were also responsible for managing other projects implemented by the RWD (such as MMGSY, PMGSY and maintenance of the road network), and could not fully commit their time to the Project. In addition, the change of the Project Director who was involved in project preparation resulted in a lack of accountability for, and ownership of, some Project activities during implementation, especially under Component 2. 54. Significant delays in implementing Component 2 activities.

The implementation of Component 2 activities was delayed by over three years due to capacity constraints in the implementing agency, prioritization of civil works, and lack of strong commitment from the implementing agency which was partly due to the changes in Project staff who were engaged in the early stages of the Project. The delay in engaging a PMC to manage the component as envisaged at preparation also contributed to further delays. The activities were initiated after a dedicated PMC was engaged in 2020. 55. Small-value contract packaging. Civil works contracts were packaged either by a single road section or in small-value packages resulting in around 600 contracts (most of which were less than US$1 million in value, while some were less than US$0.5 million in value). This strained the procurement and contract management capacity and also led to cost and time overruns. Page 21 of 49 The World Bank Bihar Rural Roads Project (P155522) 56. Procurement delays. The award of contracts for the subsequent batches of roads faced delays of over two years, caused by, inter alia, delays in finalizing the list of roads (which required various approvals within the Government), delays in reaching agreement between the Bank team and RWD on the innovative pavement methods to be used, and delays in inputs from the Bank team to finalize technical designs and in finalizing technical designs, and weak response from the market which led to several rounds of rebids.

Nevertheless, all planned contracts were signed around two years before Project closure. Factors generally subject to World Bank control 57. Supervision and reporting. Periodic progress reviews, close monitoring of disbursements, and implementation support missions helped address the challenges in project implementation. The Project MTR5 recommended that the Project be restructured to address the long delays in Component 2 implementation, by focusing on activities that could be completed by the Project closing date. This resulted in Restructuring 2, as discussed in Section B. The Bank’s supervision efforts and quality of reporting are discussed in Section IV.C. 58. Cancellations and restructurings. The Project was restructured five times as discussed in Section B. A total of US$82 million of the original credit was cancelled and the Project scope was revised due to slow progress and low disbursements. The credit closing date was extended in two stages for a total of 12 months to enable the completion of planned civil works. Factors generally outside the control of government and/or implementing entities 59. The COVID-19 pandemic. The COVID-19 pandemic during 2020 – 2022 resulted in implementation delays in civil works due to restrictions in mobility and the closure of project sites for several months. 60. Flash floods. Flash floods that occurred in several districts in 2021 affected the progress of civil works. IV.

The development outcomes of the Project are likely to be sustained, although there are some risks. GoB’s commitment to carrying forward the key infrastructure and operational improvements supported by the Project is demonstrated by the following: (i) the plan to expand the AI maintenance system to the entire network, potentially with more features on asset management; (ii) the introduction of the Bihar Rural Roads Maintenance Policy in 2018 mandating performance-based maintenance for roads completing five-year routine maintenance; (iii) the state policy on Road Safety, which mandates road safety audits for every road section that is longer than five kms; and (iv) the adoption of innovative, low cost pavement methods in the state’s MMGSY program. The key risk to the sustainability of these outcomes stems from the low institutional capacity in the road sector agencies in terms of staffing and skills. Further strengthening the skills and the staffing in these agencies is critical to sustain these outcomes and further enhance road sector management in the state. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 82. Strengthening institutions requires long term engagement and strong government commitment, and thus, a programmatic approach may be better suited for such projects.

As was evident by the Project’s experience in implementing institutional reforms, strengthening institutional processes, efficiencies, and capacities, and introducing new ways of doing business can be complex and time consuming. The lack of strong commitment from the implementing agencies along with changing political priorities can also hinder the process; this often leads to prioritizing infrastructure improvement, which are more straightforward, over institutional improvements that can be time consuming to implement and often requires strong ownerships and champions to execute. A comparative assessment carried out by the World Bank of the performance of road sector projects in the Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan in India highlights that successful implementation of key reforms in Karnataka and Anhdra Pradesh, such as adopting a road policy framework and a systematic road asset management approach, can be attributed to strong ownership, holistic approach and constant learning and innovation illustrated by the state governments. A programmatic approach, which goes beyond a typical project lifecycle, could help maintain continuous consultations and engagement with the government agencies to sensitize them to the benefits of institutional improvements and to build strong commitment over time to implement them. 83. Strong and flexible Bank support is required where the implementing agency and the sector has significant capacity gaps.

The Project was able to address the long delays, safeguards management issues, and implementation challenges faced in the first few years of the Project and expedite implementation during the latter part as a result of more handholding and targeted support from the Bank. The flexibility in the level of Bank support in response to emerging capacity shortfalls was important for the successful implementation of Project activities. In instances where significant capacity gaps are identified in the implementing agencies, such support can be built into the Project design at the beginning and options such as Hands-on Expanded Implementation Support (HEIS) can be explored for both procurement and technical support. Furthermore, considering the capacity shortfalls identified through the Project, future engagements can focus on improving the capacity of: (i) implementing agencies in relevant technical specifications, including on climate resilience Page 27 of 49 The World Bank Bihar Rural Roads Project (P155522) and road safety, to develop quality DPRs, and in supervision and monitoring of civil works; (ii) design consultants to develop quality specifications and designs; and (iii) small contractors to improve the quality of infrastructure. 84. Synergies from existing ongoing national and state level rural roads programs/ projects should be leveraged.

Based on the experience of rural road engagement at the national level and in other states, the project design incorporated the lessons learned and was built on the existing programs (PMGSY, MMGSY) including adoption of prioritization framework of investments, bidding document of PMGSY, three-tier quality monitoring mechanism, grievance redressal, contracting capacity etc. However, the execution during implementation period could have also benefitted from leveraging the institutional strengthening (e-Marg, OMMAS, new technologies) and technology adoption under the national program (PMGSY). These could also have been complimented with the learnings and results achieved in other states including Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh etc. 85. Asset and resilient management practices in the road sector can be strengthened further. The Project introduced asset and resilient management practices in the road sector.

However, there is significant potential to develop these further through: expanding the pilot AI system to a full-fledged asset management system which helps prioritize road investments in an evidence-based, systematic approach; establishment of a trained asset management unit within RWD with adequate fund allocations; implementing the recommendations of the climate vulnerability assessment and expanding it to critical sections of the road network; development of a state-level policy or guidelines to integrate climate considerations into network planning, prioritizing, technical designs and maintenance; and developing institutional capacity on both asset management and climate resilience in infrastructure. 86. Innovative road rehabilitation methods can bring benefits, but their sustainability need to be monitored over time. The Project was successful in introducing low-cost pavement methods. While these have contributed to cost reductions in the Project, their sustainability should be monitored over time based on the climatic conditions of the state and lifecycle costs, including routine and periodic maintenance. 87. Building trust through close consultations with communities can improve efficiencies in project implementation. As demonstrated by the experiences from the Janta Darbar initiative, it is clear that regular consultations with project communities play a key role in fostering trust towards the project and the implementing agencies.

Engaging community members in project activities, promptly addressing their feedback and concerns, and incorporating their suggestions are essential strategies that not only build trust but also facilitate smoother and more efficient project implementation. Such participatory approaches can be integrated into the design of future projects to enhance their effectiveness and community acceptance. 88. The adequacy and appropriateness of technology should be assessed against the specific contexts and environments in which it is used. A key lesson from the Project’s experience with the use of an app to record grievances is that when technology is used, particularly involving communities with poor literacy and inadequate access to technological devices, it is important to ensure that (i) the technology used is tailored to address the specific requirements of the users, (ii) users are aware and educated in how to use the technological solution, and (iii) the appropriateness of the use of technology is assessed in the specific context. As was evident from the Project’s experience with Janta Darbars which promoted more person-person interaction, at times, more human-oriented solutions can create better results compared to technological solutions. . KEY ISSUES & STATUS 4.1 Implementation Status and Key Decisions Progress towards achievement of the Project Development Objective (PDO) is on track, with all PDO indicators (6) having met the target. A total of 1,222 km of road receiving routine maintenance (PBC) has been completed in six project provinces. All 11 contracts (1,574.46 km) for the second three-year period (2023 – 2025) are under implementation, with physical progress at around 46-93%. For National Road 13 South (NR13S), roadworks has been under the operation and maintenance (O&M) phase. The Technical Assistance (TA) and institutional strengthening activities are almost completed. However, it is important to utilize the technical tools provided under the project (i.e., RMS, PRoMMS, IRAMS-2) to "modernize" MPWT's business process, especially with MPWT's staff shortage issue becoming more critical. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. KEY ISSUES & STATUS 4.1 Implementation Status and Key Decisions Progress towards achievement of the Project Development Objective (PDO) is on track, with all PDO indicators (6) having met the target. A total of 1,222 km of road receiving routine maintenance (PBC) has been completed in six project provinces. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL CONTEXT 1. At appraisal in 2016, Lao PDR had sustained strong economic growth, averaging around 8 percent annually since 2000, driven by natural resources, infrastructure investment, and tourism. Although poverty had declined significantly, it remained concentrated in remote and ethnic minority areas. To support continued growth and rural development, the Government sought to improve regional and domestic connectivity as part of its strategy to transform Lao PDR from a landlocked to a land-linked economy. 2. Road transport was the backbone of the economy, carrying about 98 percent of passenger traffic and 96 percent of freight. However, the road network was increasingly affected by recurrent flooding and other climate-related events, which caused significant damage, expanded maintenance backlogs, and increased reliance on costly emergency repairs. Provincial and district roads were particularly vulnerable due to lower design standards, inadequate maintenance, and limited consideration of climate risks in infrastructure design. 3.

Fiscal constraints, inadequate road resilience, and weak maintenance capacity posed significant challenges to the sustainability of the road network. Frequent climate-related damage further strained limited resources and increased reconstruction, recovery and maintenance costs. Although road asset management systems had been established for both national and provincial roads —including the Road Management System (RMS) and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS), which were introduced progressively in the early to mid-2000s under earlier road sector programs—their effectiveness was constrained by weak data, limited integration of climate risk considerations, competing investment priorities, and capacity constraints at subnational levels. 4. To address these constraints and promote inclusive growth and economic diversification, the Government of Lao People’s Democratic Republic (GoL) sought financing from the World Bank for Lao Road Sector Project II (LRSP2) to improve resilience of road network, reduce recurring disaster recovery costs, and strengthen institutional capacity to maintain road reliability. The project was designed to anchor a broader sector-wide approach, with the World Bank serving as the lead financing and coordinating partner and the Nordic Development Fund (NFD) as co-financier.

LRSP2 intentionally leveraged financing for the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Union (EU), and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), and Government road sector funding to enhance road network resilience, accessibility, and sustainability across the road sector as a whole within prioritized rural areas with high vulnerability to climate risks. To achieve these objectives, LRSP2 prioritized investment in disaster-prone rural areas in northern Lao PDR including Phongsaly, Houaphan, Oudomxay, Xiengkhouang, Xayabouly and Bolikhamxay provinces, where recurrent flash floods and slope failures frequently disrupted road connectivity. 5. LRSP2 built on the achievements of the Lao Road Sector Project (LRSP; P102398, 2010-2016). LRSP improved road conditions, established road asset management systems, strengthened road sector institutions, and enhanced rural connectivity (World Bank, 2022: 45)1. Expanding on these foundations, LRSP2 adopted a more systematic approach by integrating climate-resilient periodic maintenance into national and subnational road management systems and introducing a Contingency Emergency Response Component (CERC). The project also served as a platform for collaboration among development partners under the sector-wide approach, supporting harmonized investments and policy reforms across the road sector. LRSP2 was aligned with the World Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy for the 1 World Bank. 2022.
