LRSP2 comprised four components to strengthen road maintenance systems at both the national and provincial/district levels, contributing to improved road reliability. LRSP2 was designed to mainstream best practices by implementing a sector-wide approach to addressing the full range of road maintenance challenges through the existing government institutional structure under the coordination of a Project Coordination Committee (PCC). Component 1 focused on enhancing maintenance systems at provincial and district levels, whereas Components 2 and 3 strengthened institutional capacities and project management functions across the entire road sector. By incorporating climate resilience as a cross-cutting element under Components 2 and 4, the project also helped the Government better prepare for—and respond to—potential road damage and service disruptions caused by climate-related disasters. PDO 1 was substantially achieved based on World Bank–financed interventions, including climate resilient periodic maintenance (656 km), routine maintenance under performance-based contracts (1,574 km), and the rehabilitation and OPBRC-based operation and maintenance of NR13 South.

Implementation support was highly responsive to client needs, including the decision to drop the DLI in favor of performance-based contracting supported by independent technical audits, preparation of additional financing, and support to respond to inflation. 71. From a sustainability perspective, supervision increasingly addressed structural risks to long-term road performance.

The implementation of the Overloading Control Study, the reactivation of weight control stations, and the introduction of WIM equipment on selected sections were monitored as part of supervision. These measures helped prevent premature road deterioration and stabilize maintenance outcomes. Supervision also considered financial sustainability, including maintenance financing through the Road Fund and the medium- to long-term consideration of 13 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT demand and revenue management options, including toll systems, thereby extending the supervision focus beyond project closure. 72. Rating: Satisfactory Justification of Overall Rating of Bank Performance 73. Overall Bank performance is rated Satisfactory D. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 74. The project’s success significantly strengthening road maintenance systems has contributed to the sustainability of the road network improvements financed by the project. LRSP2 has substantially strengthened these systems asset management systems and OPBRC‑based maintenance practices within MPWT and DPWTs and the GoL continues to show strong commitment to these. Long-term sustainability of these road maintenance systems and the network depends upon stable macroeconomic conditions. 75.

The Government is continuing efforts to strengthen the sustainability of road maintenance financing through tolling and overloading charges and factoring road maintenance expenditures into the medium-term fiscal framework. While these developments do not fully resolve structural constraints, incremental steps toward improving the sustainability and institutional integration of road maintenance financing demonstrate sustained commitment. Beyond operationalizing maintenance planning and budgeting in the road sector institutions such as the Road Fund, LRSP2 has contributed to institutionalizing maintenance budgeting within the broader Laotian legal frameworks. 76. Risks to network‑level continuity are further reduced by continued parallel financing support for all operation and maintenance of all NR13 S sections under OPBRC. In addition, the preparation of the CRRCIP provides a pathway to scale up maintenance practices, climate resilience standards, and asset management systems beyond LRSP2. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 77. The project showed that performance-based maintenance (PBC/OPBRC), supported by rolling multi-year maintenance planning and road asset management systems, can deliver and sustain improvements in road condition and accessibility when embedded in government decision-making and budget processes.

Integration of climate resilience into road maintenance systems in Lao PDR resulted from a sustained commitment to building institutional, technical, and human capital and institutionalizing maintenance systems among government stakeholders and Development Partners over the past decade. These results would not have been possible without strong and consistent government commitment, sustained engagement of the World Bank and other development partners, and strong task team leadership. 78. Climate resilience proved most effective when mainstreamed across the full maintenance cycle —from design and planning to asset management and execution—resulting in fewer disruptions, lower long-term costs, and more reliable connectivity. Development Partners coordination to promote PBC was a successful strategy to keep the road infrastructure sustainability in the climate vulnerable context of Lao PDR. Rewarding the contractors for regular and timely maintenance ensured maintenance completed which improved the resilience of the road network. Early agreement on common standards, aligned schedules, and a clear coordination framework were essential to fully realize the benefits to rolling out performance-based contracting in the context of parallel financing. 14 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT 79. The project also highlights that formal emergency response mechanisms such as CERC may not always be the preferred option for governments.

In practice, the ability to respond effectively depended more on operational readiness, including pre-agreed procedures under the ERM and the use of existing contract arrangements. Project restructuring and additional financing provided flexible and timely alternatives for mobilizing resources, enabling rapid restoration of connectivity without activating CERC. 15 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT ANNEX 1. EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS 1. The efficiency analysis for the ICR of the project is based on a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) approach, which follows the same methodology at appraisal stage, including additional financing stage.

The efficiency analysis covers the time horizon of 10 years (2017-2027) for road improvements and maintenance under the original project (Component 1.1 & 1.2) and 20 years (2019-2039) for the OPBRC under Additional Financing (Component 1.5), which are based on the life cycle of actual sub-projects implemented which are road improvement. The project supported the rehabilitation of 64 km of National Road 13 North. The key assumptions include: (i) the discount rate of 12 percent; (ii) the Standard Conversion Factor (SCF) of 0.92 for investment and 0.87 for maintenance; (iii) the project could help avoid some of the emergency maintenance due to the climate resiliency improvement; and (iv) the speed improvement from 47 km/h to 70 km/h on National Roads. 2. At appraisal, the economic internal rate of return (EIRR) for Components 1.1 and 1.2 (local road improvement and maintenance) was estimated at 31.5 percent, with a net present value (NPV) of US$6.85 million. Ex-post analysis conducted in 2026 indicates an EIRR of 31.5 percent and an NPV of US$19.95 million, suggesting that economic returns for local roads were broadly maintained, with higher realized benefits reflected in the increased NPV. 3. For the full 275 km NR13 South corridor, the ex-ante economic analysis conducted under the 2019 Additional Financing estimated an overall EIRR of 26.1 percent and an NPV of US$105.54 million.

At appraisal, the corridor was structured into three sections for analytical purposes, broadly reflecting the parallel financing arrangement across development partners, though not all sections were explicitly assigned to specific financiers. During implementation, the packaging of works was restructured from three into four sections to reflect contractor capacity and facilitate timely delivery, resulting in revised section boundaries and a clearer allocation of financing among IDA, EIB, and AIIB. Ex-post results indicate an EIRR of 34.4 percent and an NPV of US$37.8 million for Section 1 (approximately 40 km) financed under the IDA credit, compared to an overall EIRR of 33.9 percent and an NPV of US$212.46 million for the full NR13S corridor. 4. This distinction reflects the underlying financing structure. While IDA financing supported Section 1 of NR13S, the economic benefits of rehabilitating and operating the full corridor were realized at the aggregate level through coordinated multi-partner implementation. Accordingly, economic efficiency can be assessed both at the level of IDA‑financed investments and at the level of overall corridor outcomes achieved through coordinated multi‑partner implementation. An analysis of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions was undertaken for NR13 South based on fuel consumption rates at different speeds under ‘with project’ and ‘without project’ scenarios. Without the project, the deteriorated condition of the roads would limit vehicle speeds, leading to higher fuel consumption (at 0.09 liter per vehicle-km) compared to the ‘with-project’ scenario. The project’s improved road condition leads to more efficient travel speeds, and hence lower fuel consumption (at 0.07 liter per vehicle-km). Gross GHG emission in the ‘with project’ scenario is 4,617,209 tCO2e3. Total net GHG emission is estimated to be −852,100tCO2e — a net reduction over the evaluation period (20 years). BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS Borrower’s Comments LRSP2 has been a priority project for the Government of the Lao PDR. The project supported a critical period of transition for the road sector from reactive, emergency-driven maintenance practices toward a systematic, data-informed, and climate-resilient approach to road asset management. The investments made under LRSP2 have directly strengthened the capacity of MPWT and its provincial departments (DPWTs) to plan, finance, and deliver road maintenance more effectively and sustainably.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: MPWT is particularly pleased with the institutionalization of the three-year rolling climate-resilient road maintenance planning process, which is now embedded in the government's annual budget preparation cycle. This reform represents a fundamental shift in how the Ministry approaches road asset management and reflects a long-term commitment to ensuring that Lao PDR's road network can withstand the growing impacts of climate change. The use of risk-informed planning tools, including the Integrated Road Asset Management System (IRAMS-2), the Road Management System (RMS), and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS) has given MPWT the institutional foundation to prioritize investments based on evidence rather than on an ad-hoc basis. The project's introduction of OPBRC on National Road 13 South contributes to the landmark achievement for the road sector in Lao PDR. NR13 South is a critical national corridor, and the OPBRC model has demonstrated that private sector pre-financing can be effectively mobilized to deliver climate-resilient rehabilitation and long-term maintenance under a single integrated contract. This modality reduces the immediate fiscal burden on government while aligning the contractor's incentives with road condition outcomes rather than volume of inputs.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Based on the success of this pilot on NR13 South under LRSP2, MPWT is committed to expanding the OPBRC approach to other priority national roads, including the ongoing NR13 North project and future operations. MPWT extends its sincere gratitude to the World Bank, the principal financier, and to the Nordic Development Fund (NDF) for their co-financing and parallel financing contributions. The Ministry acknowledges the active and consistent support provided by both partners throughout all phases of project preparation and implementation. This included technical assistance in procurement, design, and supervision; support to the development of performance-based contracting methodologies and standard bidding documents; guidance on climate resilience mainstreaming; training for MPWT and DPWT staff in PBC and OPBRC implementation, road safety audits, and environmental and social (E&S) safeguards; and close monitoring of contract implementation and safeguard compliance. This engagement was essential to the project's success and has left lasting benefits in the form of enhanced institutional capacity across the sector. MPWT also recognizes the important contribution of the NDF to the climate resilience dimensions of the project, particularly in financing climate-resilient periodic maintenance and spot improvements and the establishment of vulnerability mapping and risk-based planning tools under the RAMS/PRoMMS system.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: This support was instrumental in shifting the Ministry's planning culture from reactive emergency response to predictive, risk-informed asset management a transformation that will generate lasting dividends for the reliability and resilience of the national road network. MPWT also wishes to express its appreciation to the EIB and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) for their Page 33 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT parallel financing of sections of National Road 13 South. The participation of EIB and AIIB provided the additional scale necessary to address the full length of this critical corridor under a harmonized, performance-based contracting framework. Their adoption of the World Bank's OPBRC standards and common technical specifications ensured consistency in quality and climate resilience requirements across all sections of NR13 South, regardless of the financing source. This coordinated multi-financier approach set a strong precedent for development partner collaboration in Lao PDR's road sector, and MPWT looks forward to continued engagement with EIB and AIIB in future infrastructure initiatives.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The Ministry acknowledges that challenges were encountered during implementation, including macroeconomic pressures, particularly the sharp depreciation of the Lao Kip and inflationary trends, which reduced the real value of Road Fund counterpart financing and constrained the scope of routine maintenance deliverable under Component 1. The Ministry is committed to addressing these fiscal challenges going forward by strengthening RMF revenues, exploring supplementary financing mechanisms including potential tolling on key corridors, and continuing to advocate for adequate budget allocations for road maintenance within the national budget framework. The integration of road asset management priorities into the draft Transport Sector Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) reflects the government's commitment to sustaining and building upon the reforms introduced under LRSP2. MPWT also recognizes the progress made on road safety under LRSP2, including the approval by the Prime Minister's Office of the National Road Safety Strategy and Action Plan (2021–2030) and Action Plan (2021–2025). The Ministry will continue to pursue the implementation of this strategy and calls on development partners to sustain their engagement on road safety as a critical cross-cutting priority for the sector. Finally, MPWT wishes to acknowledge the dedication of the Project Management Unit (PMU) and all DoR and DPWT staff who contributed to the implementation of LRSP2.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Their efforts, alongside those of the World Bank and NDF teams, have delivered results well above original targets on direct beneficiaries, the rural population with access to an all-season road, and share of women in project-related paid employment. These results reflect the project's contribution not only to road connectivity but also to the broader development and inclusion goals of the government. Page 34 Official Use Only

A joint WB, AIIB, and NDF implementation support mission was conducted during June 4-17, 2021. As of May 2021, the overall physical progress achieved is 31.11%. Disbursement made so far has been limited to only a 10% advance payment, as no milestone has been fully completed. The COVID-19 outbreak has impacted the delivery of planned milestones under the Output and Performance-Based Road Contracts and overall implementation progress is approximately four months behind the schedule. The contractor’s performance has also been a factor in exacerbating the delays. The contractor needs to improve site management, mobilize additional key qualified personnel and equipment to catch up with the work program. Good progress is made on the implementation of RAP and land acquisition. As of May 31, 2021, a total of 684 grievances were recorded, mostly related to road safety concerns, dust dispersion, and slow work progress. The mission was informed that 670 of these grievances have been addressed and 14 grievances would be addressed by June 30, 2021. 6/28/2021 Page 1 of 7 The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) Road safety and traffic management need to be further improved. Luciano iv Official Use Only The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT I. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. Context at Appraisal 1. At appraisal, in 2018, Lao PDR had sustained rapid economic growth, averaging 7.8 percent annually over the preceding decade and ranked among the fastest-growing economies globally.

Growth was driven by natural resource exploitation and deeper regional integration under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), with services— particularly retail, tourism, and transport—playing an increasingly important role. Yet, this trajectory came with mounting challenges. Public debt had risen sharply, fueled in part by large-scale infrastructure investments, particularly in hydropower generation, and the Government of Lao PDR (GoL) had begun fiscal consolidation efforts, including expanding the tax base and strengthening tax administration. Further reforms were needed to enhance public investment management and address debt vulnerabilities. 2. Progress in poverty reduction was evident with absolute poverty declining from 24.6 percent in 2012 to 18.3 percent in 2018. A significant share of the population remained dependent on agriculture and highly vulnerable to shocks. Inequality persisted, reflected in a Gini index of 38.8 in 2018, while access to basic infrastructure and services, including transport—remained limited for the bottom 40 percent of the population. 3. Lao PDR’s exposure to climate and disaster risks compounded these challenges. Lao PDR is highly vulnerable to climate change due to its tropical climate, topography, and substantial poverty. Historical data showed annual expected losses from climatic events equivalent to 3–4 percent of GDP, with fiscal costs approaching 2 percent of government expenditures.

Major floods in 2013 and the 2015–16 El Niño event underscored the fragility of infrastructure, while climate projections indicated rising temperatures and more frequent extreme events, posing additional threats to economic activity and transport assets. Lao PDR ranks 142 out of 181 countries in the 2020 Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (GAIN Index), and its road infrastructure is especially at risk from climate-related events such as washouts and erosion during the rainy season. 4. Within the transport sector, the GoL prioritized large-scale infrastructure development to strengthen regional connectivity under its vision of transforming Lao PDR from landlocked to land-linked. While funding for the road sector rose to US$107 million in FY2017, allocations remained heavily skewed toward new construction and emergency repairs, contributing to rising public debt. Emergency repairs alone accounted for nearly 30 percent of the annual maintenance budget, reflecting both the impact of climate-related events and the pressing need for more resilient infrastructure. 5. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MPWT), responsible for the national road network, struggled to secure adequate and predictable financing for long-term maintenance.

The Road Fund—financed mainly through a fuel levy—expanded from US$2 million in 2002 to over US$80 million in 2016, yet its effectiveness was constrained by competing demands, weak prioritization mechanisms, and lengthy administrative procedures for budgeting, procurement, and contract management. These inefficiencies limited the adoption of a life-cycle management approach, resulting in chronic underfunding and neglected maintenance of the road network. 6. Road safety and overloading were significant concerns. Reported fatalities more than doubled between 2000 and 2010, reaching over 1,000 deaths in 2014, with motorcyclists disproportionately affected. Lao PDR recorded some of the highest GDP losses from road crashes in the region, driven by inadequate safety infrastructure, limited enforcement, and poor compliance with traffic rules. Large numbers of vehicle operators were unlicensed. Additionally, while the ASEAN standard was 11-tonne axle loads, most main roads in Lao PDR, including National Road 13 (NR13) North, were designed and built for an 8.2-tonne standard axle loads and were therefore vulnerable to damage from regional traffic. 7. At appraisal, in May 2018, improving the reliability and resilience of NR13 North was among the Ministry of Public Works and Transport’s (MPWT) key priorities.

NR13 North links the capital, Vientiane, to ten northern provinces and the Official Use Only Page 1 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT border with China, was the most heavily trafficked road in the country, and is critical to the Laotian economy, serving an important role in national and regional freight movements. Sections of NR13 North were approaching full capacity due to strong economic growth, trade expansion, and rapid growth in vehicle ownership. The road was in poor condition, with extensive pavement distress, insufficient drainage, inadequate safety features, and traffic bottlenecks particularly from Sikhai to Sikeut. Many stretches regularly flooded, disrupting traffic flow and resulting in pavement damage. 8. MPWT initially sought to reconstruct 58 km of NR13 North to a climate resilient standard under a ten-year toll road contract. Tolling met MPWT’s key objectives of ensuring efficient long-term maintenance and managing public investment costs. Although the most urbanized section from Sikhai to Sikeut was omitted from the toll proposal for socioeconomic reasons and would be improved with public financing,1 tolling was eventually rejected due to the lack of an alternative (non-tolled) route. 9. To address MPWT’s strategic priorities, an Output-and Performance-Based Road Contract (OPBRC) approach was adopted as an alternative to tolling.

OPBRC transfers construction and maintenance risks to the contractor which is paid for most – but not all – rehabilitation and improvement costs during a rehabilitation phase. Payment of the remainder is made contingent upon independent verification that contractually defined level of service standards are met over a longterm maintenance period. This model satisfied MPWT’s priorities of operationalizing a life-cycle asset management approach by creating incentives for contractors to deliver efficient and high-quality construction and preventive maintenance. OPBRC also strengthened fiscal discipline by enabling the Government to shift from short-term, ad-hoc budgeting to a multi-year, performance-driven maintenance regime with predictable costs. 10. The proposed investment in NR13 North was closely aligned with World Bank Group’s Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for Lao PDR (2017–2021). Rehabilitation and improvement of NR13 North directly supported Focus Area 1, particularly Objective 1.3: Investing in infrastructure for growth and inclusion, by improving access to all-weather roads, reducing travel time for rural populations, and supporting Road Asset Management in the road sector. It also contributed to Focus Area 3, particularly Objective 3.2: Putting in place enhanced disaster risk management and climate and disaster resilience, by integrating climate-resilient design into road rehabilitation, consistent with the CPF’s emphasis on disaster and climate resilience.

It also contributed to the Eighth National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2016– 2020) and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 9 (resilient infrastructure) and 13 (climate action). B. The Theory of Change, developed for this ICR, is grounded in the premise that targeted investments in road infrastructure, combined with innovative contracting for long-term maintenance and institutional strengthening, would lead to measurable improvements in road condition, safety, and climate resilience—contributing to resilient national and regional connectivity and inclusive economic growth in Lao PDR. 1 To manage the socioeconomic impact of tolling, GoL planned to rehabilitate a critical and densely populated 6 km link from Sikhai to Sikeut, which was within the urban area of Vientiane, with public financing; this section was therefore omitted from preparation of the toll project Official Use Only Page 2 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT Figure 1. Key assumptions are that: (A1) MPWT would continue to fund the OPBRC operations and maintenance (O&M) phase and contractors will continue to employ women in O&M phase after project closure; (A2) Institutional support would ensure sustainability beyond the project’s life; and (A3) Road users and trainees continue to use the knowledge gained from road safety campaigns and technical trainings. C. PROJECT DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES (PDOS) 13. The objective of the Project, as stated in the Project Appraisal Document and Financing Agreement, is to improve the road condition, safety and climate resilience on critical sections of National Road 13. D. KEY EXPECTED OUTCOMES AND OUTCOME INDICATORS 14. The project included three expected outcomes and corresponding outcome indicators. (a) Outcome 1, improved road condition, was monitored by the indicator ‘Reduction in vehicle operating costs (VOC) on the project road.’ (b) Outcome 2, improved road safety, was monitored by the indicator ‘Increase in average iRAP star rating of the project road.’ (c) Outcome 3, improve road climate resilience, was monitored by the indicator ‘Project road upgraded and improved with climate-resilient measures’ Official Use Only Page 3 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT E. COMPONENTS 15.

The NR13 project was structured around three interlinked components designed to address the deteriorating condition, safety risks, and climate vulnerabilities of Lao PDR’s most critical transport corridor. The project introduced the OPBRC model for the first time in the country, while also embedding climate resilience and road safety into the core of its infrastructure and institutional interventions. 16. Component 1: Road Improvement and Maintenance (Planned: US$120.5 million, including US$36.6 million from IDA; Actual: Total: US$85.5 million, including US$32 million from IDA, US$36.9 million from AIIB, US$3.6 million from NDF, and US$12.9 million from GoL). This component financed road widening, improvement, operation, and long-term maintenance of NR13 North using OPBRC. The OPBRC included a three-year rehabilitation phase followed by seven years of operations and maintenance (O&M). Eighty percent of the contract price was to be paid to the contractor during the rehabilitation phase, and repayment of the remaining capital invested in rehabilitation would be deferred and repaid on a performance-basis during the seven-year maintenance phase. The OPBRCs included climate resilience measures and promoted local women’s employment and pedestrian safety.

(d) Subcomponent 1.1: Road Improvement and Maintenance financed 64 km road improvement and maintenance of NR13 North, out of which 25 km constituted road widening and rehabilitation from 2 to 4 lanes and 39 km constituted rehabilitation along the existing right-of-way using OPBRC model. (e) Subcomponent 1.2: Land Acquisition covered land acquisition costs for road works. 17. Component 2: Technical Assistance and Supervision (Planned: US$4.8 million, including US$0.7 million from IDA; Actual: US$7.2 million, including US$2.8 million from IDA and US$4.5 million from NDF). This component supported MPWT in managing OPBRC, enhancing road safety, overloading control, and environmental/social safeguards. (f) Subcomponent 2.1: Traffic Safety, Overloading Control, and Safeguards Monitoring financed traffic safety campaigns, overloading control, and safeguards monitoring. (g) Subcomponent 2.2: Management and Supervision of OPBRC Implementation comprised the NDF-financed consultancy for supervising road works and initial O&M phase. (h) Subcomponent 2.3: Preparation of Future Investments, financed by AIIB and NDF, comprised technical, environmental, and social studies for future NR13 sections. 18. Component 3: Project Management (Planned: US$2.7 million, including US$2.7 million from IDA; Actual: US$2 million, financed by IDA).

This component provided technical and operational support for project implementation, including training, planning, financial management, procurement, M&E, and audits. 19. The project’s component structure proved robust and adaptable, enabling the delivery of high-quality infrastructure while also laying the groundwork for institutional transformation in road asset management and climateresilient transport planning. F. SIGNIFICANT CHANGES DURING IMPLEMENTATION (IF APPLICABLE) 20. Changes were introduced through an initial Level 2 Restructuring approved on April 28, 2019, and a second Level 2 Restructuring approved April 13, 2023. Revised PDOs and Outcome Targets 21. The Project’s PDO and outcome targets did not change throughout project implementation. PDO indicators did not change throughout project implementation. Revised Components 23. The second Restructuring (April 2023) expanded the scope of Component 1 Road Improvement and Maintenance to include rehabilitation, widening, and extended maintenance of an additional 6 km of NR13 North from Sikhai to Sikeut (i.e. kilometers 6-12), including road safety and climate resilience measures. Other Changes 24.

The first Restructuring (April 2019) extended the AIIB co-financing effectiveness deadline from April 30, 2019, to July 31, 2019, and adjusted the deadline for the first technical audit report to September 30, 2020. 25. The second Restructuring (April 2023), which scaled up the scope of Component 1 Road Improvement and Maintenance, also introduced the following changes to the Results Framework, project closing date, Disbursement Estimates, implementation timeline, and allocation of funds between Disbursement Categories: (a) Results Framework: The target value increased from 19 km to 24 km for the intermediate indicator ‘road upgraded from 2 to 4 lanes, with climate resilience measures’. The target values increased from 59 km to 64 km for the two intermediate indicators ‘roads rehabilitated’ and ’roads transferred to performance-based O&M phase under OPBRC’. (b) Closing Date Extension, Disbursement Estimates, and Implementation Schedule: The project’s closing date was extended by 22 months, from May 31, 2023, to March 31, 2025, and the disbursement estimates were updated to reflect the revised implementation timeline.

(c) Reallocation of Funds: Given significant cost savings for civil works costs under Component 1 Road Improvement and Management (see paragraph 31), SDR 0.92 million was reallocated from Category 1 to Category 2 to cover consultant services for supervision, environmental and social monitoring, project management, and road safety for the additional 6 km road section. Rationale for Changes and Their Implication on the Original Theory of Change 26. The rationale for the 1st restructuring (April 2019): Extension of the cross-effectiveness deadline of the AIIB loan was needed to align with AIIB’s internal approval and effectiveness timeline. The adjustment of the deadline for the first technical audit report was needed to align with the actual pace of road works implementation. 27. The rationale for the 2nd restructuring (April 2023): The second restructuring was justified by the need to expand the project to cover an additional 6 km of critical, flood-prone road from Sikeut to Sikhai. This extension would allow the GoL to complete a key missing link between central Vientiane and the project section of NR13 North, using cost savings from the original project scope. As a result, the project was able to improve a contiguous 64km section of NR13 North beginning at Sikhai, despite fiscal constraints prevented the GoL from undertaking these additional works using their own resources, as originally planned. Both restructurings reinforced the original Theory of Change. II. OUTCOME A.

RELEVANCE OF PDO Assessment of Relevance of PDOs and Rating Relevance of PDOs Official Use Only Page 5 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT 28. The PDO—to improve road condition, safety, and climate resilience on a critical section of National Road 13 North—was highly relevant to the CPFs in place at Appraisal (see paragraph 10). During implementation (2018–2025), Lao PDR experienced significant macroeconomic and fiscal deterioration, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, rising debt service obligations, and inflationary pressures. These developments constrained public investment and shifted the country’s development priorities toward fiscal sustainability, resilience, and efficiency. 29. Despite these shifts, the PDO remained highly relevant and aligned with Higher-Level Objectives (HLOs) 1 and 2 of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic - Country Partnership Framework for the Period FY2023-FY2026. Improving the condition, safety and climate resilience of NR13 North directly contributed to HLO 1: Purchasing power and access to public services protected from macroeconomic instability and fiscal pressure on social spending. Specifically, the climate resilience objective and OPBRC implementation modality supported Objective 1: Improved expenditure management and revenue mobilization, by reducing long-term emergency repair costs, reducing flood-related economic disruption, and establishing predictable maintenance costs.

The PDO also directly aligned with HLO 2: Improving labor incomes of vulnerable households and Objective 4: Increased connectivity through climate-resilient infrastructure, by improving access to markets and services for rural and peri-urban populations, particularly in floodprone areas. 30. The project’s climate-resilient design and safeguards aligned with, and supported, the government’s National Green Growth Strategy (which emphasizes addressing climate resilience and road safety) and the 9th National SocioEconomic Development Plan (NSEDP) 2021–2025. The NSEDP called for “Improving public governance and administration to be more modern, transparent and agile” (outputs 3.5) and developing “National infrastructure for regional and international integration and connectivity” (output 3.6). 31. The 2023 Restructuring, which scaled-up the use of the OPBRC contracting model and concessional financing for the additional 6 km (Sikeut–Sikhai section) of NR13 North —a known bottleneck with high exposure to flooding and traffic hazards – aligned with both the CPF and NESDP. There were no shortcomings in the relevance of the PDO to the CPF at closing, and the operation remained responsive to the country’s evolving needs. Relevance is rated High. B. ACHIEVEMENT OF PDOs (EFFICACY) Assessment of Achievement of Each Objective or Outcome 32.

Efficacy is evaluated based on the extent to which the project achieved each of the three outcomes of improving road condition, safety, and climate resilience on critical sections of National Road 13 North. The project met or surpassed outcome targets for all three PDO indicators by the closing date. 33. The project fully achieved the outcome of improving road conditions, meeting the outcome target of a 20 percent reduction in vehicle operating costs (VOC). The project funded the complete rehabilitation of the 64 km road section, using climate resilient Portland Cement Concrete (PCC) pavement through a ten-year OPBRC, which included upgrades in drainage and safety features. The project completed the original 58 km of road construction by the original closing date of May 31, 2023. This included: (i) rehabilitating and widening of 19 km from Sikeut-Songpeuay, expanding the road from 2 to 4 lanes, (ii) fully rehabilitating the 39 km two-lane road section from SongpeuayPhonhong, and (iii) initiating the O&M phase. Rehabilitation and widening of the 6 km Sikhai–Sikeut section from 2 to 4 lanes was completed, and the O&M phase was initiated, before the revised closing date of March 31, 2025. 34. The project road works have resulted in lasting improvement to the condition of the road pavement.

Prior to rehabilitation, the average International Roughness Index (IRI)2 was 7.0 m/km along the original 58 km section and 2 International Roughness Index is an internationally recognized measure of ride quality, fuel efficiency, and vehicle maintenance costs. Official Use Only Page 6 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT 6.5 m/km along the additional 6 km. At project closing, the IRI had improved to 3.2 m/km and 2.7 m/km, respectively. Upon closing of the project, as a result of the improved pavement, VOC along the project corridor (64 km) fell from US$0.36 per vehicle-kilometer, in the business-as-usual scenario, to US$0.29 per vehicle-kilometer, under the project scenario, according to fuel consumption (survey) data collected during implementation3. 35. Travel time improved significantly, although it was not measured and tracked as a separate indicator in the Results Framework (RF) or accounted in the estimated reduction in VOC. On the original 58 km section, average travel time decreased from 120 minutes (~29 km/h), before the project, to less than 60 minutes (~58 km/h), at project closing. On the additional 6 km Sikhai–Sikeut section, travel time was reduced from 25 minutes to less than 10 minutes. These improvements reflect the impact of lower road roughness, better road geometry, reduced flooding and closures, and improved traffic management. 36.

Road user feedback can offer a more user-centric and holistic view of road condition improvement. A road user satisfaction survey conducted at project closing found that 91 percent of respondents expressed satisfaction with the improved road condition, mentioning smoother travel, reduced travel time, and fewer vehicle breakdowns as key benefits. 37. The OPBRC model used for these road works ensured that road condition standards were maintained throughout implementation and will continue to be upheld during the seven-year maintenance phase, which goes well beyond the project closing date (see paragraphs 52 and 87). 38. The project achieved the objective of improving safety along the NR13 North corridor and met the target for the PDO indicator “Increase in average iRAP star rating of the project road”. The average iRAP star rating4 rose from 1 Star at baseline to 3 Stars at closing, meeting the end target for both vehicle occupants and motorcyclists. A 2023 iRAP survey of the original 58 km section showed that 100 percent of the corridor was rated above 3 Stars for vehicle occupant and motorcyclist safety, compared to only 32 percent and 5 percent, respectively, before the project. Road safety interventions implemented under the project were adopted following a detailed road safety audit to identify optimal interventions.

The iRAP results reflect substantial safety gains from a comprehensive package of interventions, including road widening, improved alignment, guardrails, reflective markers, rumble strips, delineators, pedestrian facilities (crossings, sidewalks, speed-calming in high-risk areas), and upgraded signage and markings -- as well as long-term maintenance of safety improvements. 39. Although pedestrian ratings were largely unmeasured due to minimal pedestrian activity at the time of iRAP surveys, a post-construction beneficiary survey found 92 percent of respondents believed that the road was safer for pedestrians—higher than for vehicle occupants (82 percent) and motorcyclists (77 percent). Star rating for bicycles was not reported in project documents. Road safety interventions carried out on the additional 6 km road section were similar to the original 58 km road section, although the iRAP survey was limited to the original road. 40. Beyond infrastructure improvements, the project contributed to safer road user behavior through extensive awareness and enforcement measures led by a dedicated Road Safety Taskforce. While not tracked in the results 3 Due to variation in fuel costs, savings declined from 25 percent at completion of the project civil works to 20 percent at closing.

The iRAP star rating is a road safety assessment measure from the International Road Assessment Programme (iRAP) that rates road sections from 1 to 5 stars based on the safety they offer to different road users — vehicle occupants, motorcyclists, pedestrians, and bicyclists. Star ratings connotate: 5 Stars – Safest: Road has features that greatly reduce the likelihood and severity of crashes (e.g., divided carriageway, wide sealed shoulders, protected pedestrian crossings, safe speeds). 4 Stars – Safe: Most road safety features in place, some remaining risks. 3 Stars – Acceptable: Basic safety features but significant risks remain in certain scenarios. 2 Stars – Poor: Few safety features; higher crash likelihood and severity. 1 Star – Least safe: Very high risk; minimal or no safety features. 4 Official Use Only Page 7 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT framework, these efforts included 63 school campaigns reaching over 9,800 students (45 percent girls), 31 enforcement campaigns with local police, and additional initiatives such as social media outreach, village loudspeaker announcements, radio messages, roadside billboards, portable warning signage, motorcycle safety training delivered to students in the schools along the roads, and strengthened road safety enforcement along the corridor. 41.

The project achieved the intended outcome of improving climate resilience of the project road and fully achieved the target for the PDO indicator “Project road upgraded and improved, with climate resilient measures”. Climate-resilient design elements identified during the preparation phase primarily focused on addressing flooding in low-lying areas including raising the road profile and improving drainage so that traffic is less likely to be interrupted during flood events and installing PCC pavement which can withstand overtopping. Additional measures included enhancing water-crossing structures and side drainage, strengthening bridge approaches, slope protection, and reinforcing culvert inlets and outlets throughout the entire road corridor. The project responded dynamically to evolving climate risks, particularly the increased flooding caused by the parallel Lao-China Railway and Vientiane– Vang Vieng Expressway. Design adjustments were made to accommodate these changes, including additional culverts and raised profiles. These measures were integrated into engineering design and implemented as per specifications. 42. An independent compliance assessment was conducted to verify that climate resilience elements of the design were implemented according to specifications and of sufficient quality.

The technical audit findings confirmed that the road was designed and constructed to climate-resilient standards, which incorporate engineered solutions, with approximately 33.7 percent of total construction costs directly attributable to those measures. Justification of Overall Efficacy Rating 43. Rating: High. The project fully achieved the three PDO outcomes. Causal links between project activities and observed outcomes are well established by clear evidence. C. EFFICIENCY 44. Economic efficiency and use of resources exceeded norms in the road sector in Lao PDR. Project management and implementation were efficient, with no major delays or cost overruns despite numerous challenges such as the COVID-19 pandemic, high inflation, and adoption of a new and complex road works contracting approach (OPBRC). The original project scope and PDO outcomes were achieved prior to the original project closing date of May 31, 2023, and significantly below budget. Extension of the project closing date was undertaken solely to complete the 6 km scale-up road works (see paragraphs 34 and 68). 45. Strong market interest generated cost savings of 23 percent (US$17.5 million) for the original scope of civil works. These savings enabled the inclusion of an additional 6 km of road improvement works (Sikhai–Sikeut section) via Restructuring in 2023. This section was widened from 2 to 4 lanes and improved with climate resilience and safety features through a third OPBRC procurement.

Despite expanding the scope to rehabilitation and improvement of 64 km, Component 1 costs remained below original estimates. 46. The ex post economic evaluation found the project’s economic efficiency exceeded estimates at appraisal due to the lower actual investment cost and the high benefits from improving the additional 6 km high-traffic road section. Ex-post economic analysis found that the scaled-up project comprising the 64 km from Sikhai to Phonhong produced a Net Present Value (NPV) of 39.2 percent and Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of US$180 million (see Annex 4), fifty percent higher than the appraisal estimates of 26.3 percent and US$121.97 million, respectively. Key economic benefits of the project are from lower vehicle operating costs (VOC) due to the improved road conditions, reduced travel time, lower emergency repair and maintenance costs, value of timesaving for freight, and reduced road collision costs. Official Use Only Page 8 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT 47. A value for money analysis found that use of the OPBRC modality itself contributed to efficiency above norms for road works of similar scope and scale in Lao PDR. The analysis shows that the EIRR of OPBRC (39.2 percent) is 5.6 percent higher than the estimated counterfactual scenario in which traditional road contracting was used (with estimated EIRR of 33.7 percent).

The Benefit-Cost (B/C) ratio is 4.5 and 2.2 for OPBRC and conventional contract, respectively. Assessment of Efficiency and Rating 48. Efficiency is rated High considering the high economic benefits, cost-effective use of resources, and successful adaptation to implementation challenges. D. JUSTIFICATION OF OVERALL OUTCOME RATING 49. The overall outcome rating is Highly Satisfactory given the ratings of High for Relevance, Efficacy, and Efficiency. E. OTHER OUTCOMES AND IMPACTS (IF ANY) Gender 50. The project delivered strong benefits for women. Out of the 605,000 direct beneficiaries, 56 percent were women. Gender-sensitive design and monitoring measures were incorporated, such as pedestrian safety improvements near markets and schools, which disproportionately benefited women traders and schoolchildren. Women also participated directly in project-related employment: under the OPBRC, the share of women employed in paid jobs reached 35 percent, and as high as 61 percent during the first year of maintenance—far exceeding the original target of 15 percent. The grievance redress mechanism (GRM), which disaggregated complaints and feedback by gender, further ensured that women’s voices were systematically captured and addressed during implementation. Institutional Strengthening 51.

The project made major contributions to building institutional capacity within the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MPWT), especially in contract management, safeguards compliance, performance-based road maintenance, and life-cycle asset management. The project not only piloted OPBRC but also institutionalized its use by developing a standardized bidding document, embedding performance standards and service-level requirements in the contract, preparing a Sustainability Plan and an O&M plan, establishing an O&M unit within the Department of Roads (DoR), delivering extensive training to MPWT staff and the contracting industry, and procuring specialized equipment (e.g., laser profiler) to monitor service levels. These measures established the institutional framework and capacity required for scaling-up OPBRC and monitoring the O&M phase beyond project closing date. While not explicitly captured in the PDO, institutional strengthening for long-term maintenance planning, predictable budgeting, and life-cycle asset management practices is one of the project’s most significant outcomes. 52. Crucially, the OPBRC model piloted under NR13 North has been endorsed by the Government and is now being applied to additional national roads and by other development partners.

Lessons from NR13 North have been shared regionally with peers in Cambodia, Mongolia, and other countries, positioning Lao PDR as an early adopter of performance-based road contracting in the region and underscoring OPBRC’s value as a replicable model for sustainable asset management. Mobilizing Private Sector Financing 53. Private sector investment was undertaken through the OPBRC modality. A portion of the capital invested in road rehabilitation is being repaid on a performance basis using counterpart financing during the ongoing seven-year maintenance phase from March 2023 to March 2030. Lao PDR continues to mobilize further private sector investment through additional OPBRCs (see paragraph 53). In tandem, sector dialogue during implementation has supported GoL to explore additional road user fee mechanisms to fund long-term maintenance contracts (see paragraph 87). Creating Official Use Only Page 9 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT opportunities for domestic contractors to participate in road maintenance at this higher technical and managerial level has also helped develop private sector capacity for similar projects in the future. Poverty Reduction and Shared Prosperity 54. The broader socio-economic impacts of the project were evident along the NR13 North corridor at closing.

Improving road condition, safety, and reliability of NR13 North has reduced travel times and vehicle operating costs, lowering the cost of goods and services while improving access. 68 percent of Beneficiary Survey respondents reported that the improved road helped reduce poverty by increasing access to jobs, schools, and markets. These impacts were especially significant for low-income households that depend on road transport for their livelihoods and daily needs. 55. Business expansion was evident along the rehabilitated corridor, with new shops, service providers, and larger commercial establishments (e.g., vehicle dealers, equipment rental, bulk distributors) occupying previously underutilized land. In Lak 52 village of Phonhong District, land prices increased by 150 percent compared to the pre-project period, signaling heightened attractiveness for investment. This urbanization, visible in satellite imagery, highlighted the project’s transformative economic impact, while also creating new demands for urban drainage and land-use planning. 56. The OPBRC contract format generates a combination of other direct indirect economic benefits. The contractor employed up to 700 laborers during rehabilitation, a significant share of whom were unskilled local workers. Depending on seasonal requirements, between 54 and 81 individuals were employed in year one of the seven-year maintenance period, providing stable incomes and building local skills.

Incorporating climate resilience into infrastructure design reduces future emergency repair costs and enables more efficient management of infrastructure, supporting sustained long-term economic growth. Other Unintended Outcomes and Impacts 57. The project delivered important environmental and climate co-benefits. The Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMPs) helped identify strategies to mitigate construction-related impacts - such as dust, noise, and erosion - while raising awareness of environmental safeguards among contractors and local communities. III. KEY FACTORS AFFECTED IMPLEMENTATION AND OUTCOME A. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 58. A well-structured and simple project design. The project’s development objectives were realistic and clearly defined, and the OPBRC approach was well-aligned to MPWT’s road sector strategies and GoL’s national priorities, and the design of key activities was simple, with only two civil works packages. An assessment of lifecycle costs for pavement options identified PCC pavement as more durable and cost effective. Implementation support strategies such the Technical Audit and Sustainability Plan were appropriate to strengthen monitoring and sustainability, respectively. 59. The toll road proposal.

Although improvement of the Sikhai-Sikeut road section was a high priority of the Government, the toll road project excluded this section when conceptual designs and environmental and social (E&S) instruments were prepared and was therefore excluded from the scope of OPBRC bidding documents. 60. Close Development Partner coordination. World Bank support for preparation of technical and E&S requirements helped mobilize additional financial resources from AIIB and NDF. Preparation anticipated challenges related to land acquisition, safeguards, and contractor capacity, and included mitigation measures such as financing for a Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) for resettlement under the NDF Grant. Implementation benefitted from alignment of load control and road safety interventions with ongoing programs supported by IDA, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), and German Development Bank (KfW). Official Use Only Page 10 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION Factors Subject to Government and Implementing Entity Control 61. Implementing entity coordination. The Project Management Unit (PMU) and Department of Roads (DoR) maintained strong coordination with key stakeholders including contractors, local authorities, supervision consultants, and Project Affected People.

Despite the large scale of resettlement in the densely populated project area, the PMU was adequately staffed and resettlement was implemented efficiently, in part due to the quality of the GRM mechanism. 62. Strong MPWT commitment. MPWT leadership was committed to strengthening maintenance efficiency. Technical training and awareness-raising built agency capacity and consensus around the OPBRC model. The establishment of a Road Safety Taskforce and integration of climate-resilient design elements demonstrated leadership. 63. Adaptive management. The OPBRC model introduced new demands on contract administration, including performance monitoring, dispute resolution, and payment certification. Gaps in contract clarity and institutional capacity were evident. MPWT’s readiness to upskill and adapt was critical to overcoming early implementation challenges—such as unclear performance indicators, limited contractor familiarity, and weak contract management systems. 64. Market outreach. Extensive market outreach and training to contractors informed the OPBRC contract design and contributed to strong market interest – with 32 firms submitting bids – and significant cost savings. Savings enabled the project to be scaled up, while remaining within budget (see paragraphs 24 and 46). Factors Subject to World Bank Control 65. Supervision and support.

The World Bank provided consistent supervision, including regular technical meetings, technical missions, and feedback on Government’s completion report. TTLs and sector specialists engaged regularly with the PMU, offering guidance on safeguards, procurement, and economic analysis. 66. Adaptation to changing conditions. The World Bank responded flexibly to emerging challenges, including adjusting designs due to increased flooding risks from adjacent infrastructure and minimizing resettlement impact without compromising cost-effectiveness. Factors Outside the Control of Government and Implementing Entities 67. COVID-19 Pandemic, inflation, and exchange rate fluctuations. Delays due to pandemic-related movement restrictions, supply chain disruptions, and reduced contractor capacity were mitigated through close monitoring of the contractor, increased reliance on local resources, and weekly virtual implementation support by the World Bank, AIIB, and NDF. Amid inflation and exchange rate fluctuations, uncertainties about the pandemic’s impact on project costs led to delays in the decision to scale up the project. As a result, the project’s closing date had to be extended by several months. 68. Infrastructure Interdependencies. The construction of the Lao-China Railway and Vientiane–Vang Vieng Expressway altered runoff patterns and introduced new flooding risks that required additional culverts and raised profiles along NR13 North.

While these design modifications led to only modest cost increases, they significantly enhanced the road’s resilience in response to the changing environment. IV. BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME A. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) Official Use Only Page 11 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT M&E Design 69. The M&E design was underpinned by a focused PDO, clear description of the results chain, and appropriate PDO indicators to monitor each of the three outcome areas. The PDO indicators were clearly defined, measurable, and directly attributable to the project, providing a strong evidence base for monitoring project outcomes. They included both quantitative measures – such as IRI, VOC, iRAP ratings - and qualitative evidence, including beneficiary surveys and Technical Audits to verify that resilience measures were constructed according to specifications. A minor limitation is that the PDO indicator for resilience could have been improved by tracking the completion rate (percentage) of resilience interventions. 70. The intermediate indicators were thoughtfully designed to effectively track and monitor physical outputs (e.g., kilometers of road upgraded or rehabilitated), gender inclusion (e.g., share of women employed), institutional strengthening (e.g., staff trained on OPBRC), and sustainability (e.g., kilometers of road under performance-based O&M).

These were also specific, measurable, and time-bound, with baselines and targets clearly defined at appraisal. Disaggregation by gender was applied to beneficiaries, grievances, and training participants, reflecting the project’s emphasis on inclusive development. It could have been beneficial to include intermediate indicators for monitoring training and overloading control. M&E Implementation 71. The M&E implementation was consistent and technically sound. The MPWT, supported by the supervision consultant, collected and reported data regularly. The results framework was updated during the 2023 restructuring to reflect the expanded scope (an additional 6 km of road), and the revised indicators were tracked accordingly. The project also maintained a functioning GRM, which contributed to monitoring social impacts. Accurate results monitoring, safeguards reporting, and field supervision provided a robust evidence base for assessing outcomes. M&E Utilization 72. M&E data were actively used to inform project management and decision-making. For example, the identification of cost savings led to the 2023 restructuring, which expanded the project scope and extended the closing date. The M&E system also supported safeguards compliance by tracking grievances and contractors’ workforce trained in Environmental, Social, Health and Safety (ESHS), Occupational Health and Safety (OHS), and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Code of Conducts.

The use of performance-based indicators under the OPBRC model reinforced accountability and continuous monitoring of road condition and service levels. The project’s results were well documented and substantiated by field data, which informed preparation of the borrower’s completion report and the World Bank’s ICR. Justification of Overall Rating of Quality of M&E 73. The M&E system was well designed, effectively implemented, and actively used to guide project decisions. There were no significant shortcomings in any of the three dimensions. The quality of M&E is rated High. B. ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND FIDUCIARY COMPLIANCE 74. The project complied with all applicable environmental, social, and fiduciary requirements throughout implementation, with moderate challenges that were effectively addressed. 75. The project involved substantial civil works along the NR13 North corridor and is classified as Category A under the World Bank’s Operations Policy 4.01 Environmental Assessment. An Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) and Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) were prepared, disclosed, and implemented. These were updated during the 2023 restructuring to include the additional 6 km section (Sikeut–Sikhai), which traverses a densely populated urban area.

Environmental risks such as dust, noise, erosion, and construction waste were mitigated through standard measures, Official Use Only Page 12 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT with compliance monitored by the supervision consultant and MPWT’s Environment and Social Division (ESD). No major environmental incidents were reported. Social Safeguards and Road Safety 76. The Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was successfully implemented across the full 64 km corridor, covering both the original 58 km and the additional 6 km added during restructuring. Despite affecting over 5,200 households and facing COVID19-related disruptions, compensation and relocation activities were completed in a timely and policy-compliant manner. The engineering designs were prepared in a way to minimize land acquisition impacts. The GRM resolved over 890 grievances, a large portion of which were queries related to resettlement, and the Ethnic Group Engagement Plan (EGEP) ensured culturally appropriate engagement with ethnic communities. 77. A minor shortcoming was noted in the delayed finalization of land titling for project-affected households, which required a post-completion action plan. While compensation was completed, the modification of land titles lagged due to internal government processes and is expected to be completed by November 2025. This did not materially affect the overall supervision quality or the achievement of development outcomes. 78.

Road safety emerged as a critical concern during implementation. Several traffic collisions occurred, including fatalities in 2020, 2021, and 2022, prompting detailed Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and the development of Safeguards Corrective Action Plans (SCAP). These investigations revealed contributing factors such as poor road conditions, inadequate signage, insufficient lighting, and driver negligence. In response, the project implemented a range of safety measures including improved signage, lighting, and road maintenance. A dedicated Road Safety Engineer was assigned, and traffic management plans were incorporated into the ESMP and monitored monthly by the supervision consultant. Fiduciary Compliance 79. Financial Management (FM) and procurement arrangements were implemented in accordance with World Bank guidelines. The project maintained adequate financial records, submitted timely interim unaudited financial reports (IUFRs), and received unqualified audit opinions throughout the implementation period. Procurement was carried out using World Bank procedures, and the OPBRC was competitively tendered. While the project experienced some delays in contract execution due to market volatility and currency depreciation, these were managed through contract amendments and close supervision. The fiduciary performance of the project was rated Satisfactory. C. BANK PERFORMANCE Quality at Entry 80. The World Bank’s performance during preparation was highly satisfactory.

Recognizing impediments to the proposed toll road, the World Bank supported MPWT to identify an alternative project design that strategically aligned with Lao PDR’s priorities and the World Bank’s engagement objectives. While focusing on improving road condition, safety, and climate resilience along a critical national corridor, the project design indirectly facilitated long-term institutional development priorities related to maintenance. Introducing the OPBRC—the first of its kind in Lao PDR— reflected a forward-looking and innovative approach to road asset management. The World Bank used its convening power effectively to bring together multiple financiers—AIIB and NDF—under a coordinated framework, leveraging complementary expertise and financing. This was the first project in the EAP transport portfolio to mobilize co-financing from AIIB. 81. The project design was technically robust, incorporating climate adaptation measures such as raised road profiles and high-capacity drainage systems. A World Bank comparison of lifecycle costs identified PCC as the most costeffective pavement option. Environmental and social safeguards were integrated early, with a Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) and a functioning GRM in place.

The project also embedded gender-sensitive design elements, including improved Official Use Only Page 13 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT pedestrian facilities near markets and schools, and achieved 35 percent female employment target under OPBRC implementation. Fiduciary and procurement arrangements were sound, and the results framework was realistic, practical, and measurable. Implementation arrangements were embedded within existing institutional structures, and risks were appropriately identified and mitigated. While the complexity of the OPBRC model and the land titling process required sustained attention during implementation, these were well anticipated and addressed through early design and institutional engagement. Rating: Highly Satisfactory. Quality of Supervision 82. The World Bank’s supervision of the NR13 project was proactive, consistent, and technically strong. The World Bank maintained close engagement with the client and development partners throughout implementation, conducting regular implementation support missions, bi-weekly technical meetings, and field visits. Coordination with co-financiers — AIIB and NDF — through joint missions was a notable strength which enabled streamlined and harmonized support to the Government, reduced transaction costs for the implementing agencies, and ensured consistent messaging and alignment across development partners.

Performance reporting was candid and action-oriented, and the World Bank’s engagement contributed significantly to the project’s timely completion and achievement of its development outcomes. 83. The project’s turnaround from a Substantial-risk operation to a strong performer was driven by consistent leadership and the presence of the World Bank’s Country Office. Their contextual knowledge, language fluency, and longterm engagement enabled agile responses to evolving challenges, including procurement delays, safeguard complexities, and external shocks such as COVID-19 and flooding. This continuity proved essential for maintaining momentum and ensuring effective coordination across central and provincial levels. 84. Strategic use of restructurings and support to the OPBRC model significantly expanded the project’s impact. The inclusion of an additional 6 km of road improvements and full utilization of project savings increased the project’s economic benefits (see paragraph 47). The World Bank played a key role in enhancing the quality of OPBRC bid documents by mobilizing an international expert. World Bank support for the Sustainability Plan and Maintenance Plan and overall institutionalization of OPBRC has contributed to sustainability (see paragraphs 52 and 87). Rating: Highly Satisfactory Justification of Overall Rating of Bank Performance 85. The World Bank’s overall performance is rated Highly Satisfactory.

Preparation was highly satisfactory, with strong strategic alignment, sound technical design, and effective integration of safeguards, fiduciary, and institutional arrangements. Supervision was proactive and well-coordinated with co-financiers. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 86. Institutional capacity strengthening and sector dialogue provided strong support to sustainability. MPWT has established the capacity to independently implement the remainder of the ongoing seven-year maintenance phase (see paragraph 52). The success of the OPBRC demonstration, presented to the National Assembly, has contributed to scaling up to ten ongoing OPBRC contracts. In parallel, MPWT has stepped-up efforts to generate funding through user charges, including an initial focus on tolling truck traffic on NR13 South which may expand to NR13 North. A new axel load control station is planned on NR13 North in addition to reactivation of the existing station. 87. Despite these efforts, the ability to fully fund road network maintenance remains challenged by limited resources and high emergency repair costs, which pose a moderate risk to the sustainability of project outcomes. The recent Lao Road Sector Financing ASA revealed that, over the past four years, average annual road network investment was Official Use Only Page 14 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT US$152.5 million, including most Development Partner contributions for the road sector.

This amount is less than half of the optimal funding required to meet network needs over the next five years. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 88. A simple and flexible project design and scalable PDO and indicators facilitated implementation and responsiveness to evolving development needs. The project design consisting of a few key contracts reduced transaction costs and enabled the client to focus resources and attention adapting to the OPBRC contract format and addressing other implementation challenges. Easing into the OPBRC approach was particularly important given capacity constraints within the country context. The PDO and outcome indicators were simple and readily scalable, allowing for adjustments to mitigate risks such as potential cost escalations, as well as to capitalize on opportunities like scale-up restructuring. 89. Strong client commitment, hands-on support, proactive training, strategic market engagement, and robust technical support were critical to the successful roll-out of OPBRC contracting. Implementing Agency ownership of the demonstration OPBRC at the Ministerial level was a critical factor contributing to rapid institutionalization through training, acquisition of monitoring equipment, and establishment of a monitoring unit.

Timely market outreach and training of contractors increased their understanding of the OPBRC model and collected feedback on key contract parameters – such as the proportion of contract costs to be paid during the maintenance period – leading to a stronger market response. The World Bank’s support to mobilizing an international performance-based contracting expert contributed to the high quality of OPBRC bidding documents. These experiences highlighted the need for tailored capacity-building, iterative contract refinement, and sustained technical support. 90. Close Development Partner coordination strengthened the project design, implementation, and impact. Financing and implementation support from IDA, AIIB, and NDF for works, resettlement, and supervision, enabled the project to achieve greater scale and impact, in line with development partner priorities. The project approach to Road safety and Axel Load control was designed and implemented according to ongoing programs supported by IDA, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), and German Development Bank (KfW). Close cooperation between the World Bank, AIIB, and NDF provided strong implementation support to the Implementing Agency, MPWT. The alignment of financing and technical support demonstrated that coordinated development finance can amplify impact beyond tangible physical outputs.

Page 23 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT ANNEX 4. EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS 1. The efficiency analysis for the ICR of the project is based on a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) approach, which follows the same methodology at appraisal stage. The efficiency analysis covers the time horizon of 30 years (2018-2047), based on the life cycle of actual sub-projects implemented which are road improvement. The project supported the rehabilitation of 64 km of National Road 13 North.

The key assumptions include: (i) the discount rate of 12 percent; (ii) the Standard Conversion Factor (SCF) of 0.92 for investment and 0.87 for maintenance; (iii) the project could help avoid some of the emergency maintenance due to the climate resiliency improvement; (iv) the speed improvement from 30 km/h to 60 km/h; and, (v) traffic growth of 3 percent (until 2025, and 2 percent afterward). 2. At appraisal, the EIRR was estimated at 26.3%, with a net present value (NPV) of US$121.97 million. The ex-post analysis conducted 2025 for the 58 km Sikeut–Phonhong and 6 km Sikhai–Sikeut sections revealed significantly stronger performance with an overall EIRR at 38.5% and NPV of US$180 million. 3. Key economic benefits are from lower vehicle operating costs (VOC) due to the improved road conditions, reduced travel time, reduced emergency repair costs, value of time saving for freight delays, and reduced road accidents. The economic internal rate of return (EIRR) at completion is estimated at 38.5% with net present value (NPV) of US$180 million. The project’s EIRR is higher than the level envisioned at appraisal due to the lower actual investment cost and the additional 6 km of road improvement (with high traffic volume). This provides larger benefits from VOC and VOT savings, and that the economic analysis at appraisal was more conservative with some of the improvement assumptions. Figure A4.1 shows the share of the economic benefits.

The majority of the economic benefits are from the reduction of VOT (50%) and VOC (44%). Figure 4A.1: Share of the economic benefits Freight Travel Time Savings (VOD) 2% Road Accidents 2% Economic EM cost avoided 2% VOC Savings 44% Pax Travel Time Saving (VOT) 50% 4. Competitive procurement generated notable cost savings. Civil works bid prices were approximately 30% lower than the engineer’s cost estimates, resulting in savings of around US$12 million. These savings enabled the inclusion of an additional 6 km of road improvement works (Sikhai–Sikeut section), which was widened from two to four lanes. Despite Page 24 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT the expanded scope, Component 1 remained below its originally allocated budget. As a result, the EIRR increased from 26% to 39% as the road rehabilitation length increased from 58 km to 64 km. 5. An analysis of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions was undertaken based on fuel consumption rates at different speeds under ‘with project’ and ‘without project’ scenarios. Without the project, the deteriorated condition of the roads would limit vehicle speeds, leading to higher fuel consumption per vehicle-km compared to the ‘with-project’ scenario. The project’s improved road condition leads to more efficient travel speeds, and hence lower fuel consumption. Gross GHG emission in the ‘with project’ scenario is 2,638,753 tCO2e.

Total net GHG emission is estimated to be −447,478tCO2e — a net reduction over the evaluation period (30 years). The annual average net GHG emission is −14,916tCO2e per year. The social benefit from GHG reduction is estimated to be US$34 million, based on social cost of emission reduction from the World Bank’s Guidance Note on Shadow Price of Carbon in Economic Analysis (2024). 6. The project length was extended by 22 months; however, the time extension helped the project be more economically efficient. The extended project duration allowed more time for stakeholder engagement, safeguards resolution, and the inclusion of additional high impact works. The longer time also allowed the project to complete an additional 6 km, which added to the benefits without additional costs to the project. By project close, the full 64 km corridor had been upgraded or rehabilitated, exceeding the scope envisaged at appraisal. The overall efficiency for this project is rated High. The NR13 Section, which received project financing, is a critical segment serving the highest traffic volume and providing a vital connection between Vientiane Capital and the northern part of the country.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: As a backbone route spanning from the Chinese border to the Cambodian border, NR13 plays an essential role in national connectivity. The OPBRC model has demonstrated improved efficiency in road development and maintenance, leading MPWT to expand its application to other roads including NR13 South (five contracts), NR2 under SEAREC (five contracts), and additional forthcoming projects. MPWT extends its gratitude to the World Bank, the principal donor, as well as AIIB and NDF for their co-financing and parallel financing respectively contributions to this initiative. The Ministry acknowledges their active support throughout project preparation and implementation, including market sounding, OPBRC training, development of financing structures, standard bidding documentation, service level specifications, procurement processes, and the preparation of safeguard instruments such as the Resettlement Action Plan and ESMP, alongside traffic management plans and close monitoring of contract implementation, safeguard compliance, and RAP execution. These efforts were instrumental in ensuring project success. In addition to financial support, the donors provided valuable guidance that strengthened the capacity of MPWT and the local contracting industry regarding OPBRC preparation and implementation. To promote the long-term sustainability of this OPBRC contract, MPWT has developed a comprehensive sustainability plan.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: This plan includes appropriate budget allocation for the O&M phase and establishes institutional arrangements for OPBRC contract management through the end of the contract. Specifically, an OPBRC unit has been established under DoR to oversee all aspects of OPBRC contract administration.
